activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: Under the legal rule called contra proferentem, used in many jurisdictions, an ambiguous term in a contract is usually read against the party that wrote it.
story:
Rosalie opened her laptop at the kitchen table while her mother made tea, because the email had come at 4:51 and the deadline said 5:00, and she was not going to lose eighty dollars to a clock.

The charge sat on her bill like a splinter: "Device upgrade fee, applicable per applicable term." Her mother had said phone companies do this to everyone, pay it, and Rosalie had almost paid it. Then she read the line again. Per applicable term. Which term? The contract ran twelve pages, and she had signed it in September with her thumb on the phone screen, the way you sign everything now, no pen, no ceremony, just a name typed into a box.

She found the live chat button and typed: I'm disputing the upgrade fee. The line about applicable terms is unclear.

A representative named Devon answered. He said the fee was standard. She asked, "Standard according to which term, exactly?" He pasted the same sentence back at her. She asked for the contract's plain-language summary. He said the contract governed. He was pasting faster than she was reading, and her mother's kettle was screaming in the other room.

Zakaria was online, so she messaged him. His father fixed contracts for a living, some kind of compliance job, and Zakaria had absorbed things the way kids absorb a parent's second language, without grammar, fluently. "Ambiguous line?" he typed. "Who wrote the contract, you or them?" She typed: "Them, obviously." He sent back one word, then the rest of it. "Contra proferentem. My dad says it a lot. An unclear term gets read against whoever wrote it."

Rosalie copied the words into the chat with Devon. She wrote: Under the rule called contra proferentem, an ambiguous term in a contract is read against the party that wrote it. Your company wrote this contract. Read the fee line in my favor and remove the charge. Her hands were damp on the trackpad. It felt absurd, pasting law at a man named Devon, the way it felt absurd to raise your hand in a class where nobody else was speaking.

Devon's reply took four minutes, long enough for her mother to come in with two mugs and for Rosalie to explain, fast, in a low voice, what the charge was and what she had just sent. Her mother read over her shoulder. "You learned that where?" she asked, and Rosalie said, "Zakaria," and her mother made a sound that was not quite approval and not quite doubt, and sat down.

Devon wrote: I've escalated your case to our billing review team. As a courtesy, the fee has been waived. The word courtesy snagged at Rosalie, a little hook of rectitude. It was not a courtesy. It was not goodwill, and it was not them being nice. They had written something equivocal and gotten caught at it, and now they were dressing the retreat in the language of a favor. She typed: Thank you, then deleted it and typed: I accept the waiver, and pressed send. Her mother raised her mug slightly, like a toast or a surrender.

But lying in bed that night, phone on her chest, Rosalie turned the whole thing over and it would not settle. Devon had folded in four minutes, which meant either the rule was that strong or the fee was that worthless, and she could not tell which. If the rule were that strong, why was the sentence still in the contract, waiting for the next sixteen-year-old who would not know the words? If the fee were that worthless, why had they billed it at all? She understood that she had won something without understanding the size of the thing she had won, and that the company could metastasize the same ambiguity into next month's bill under a different name, and she would have to find the words again. Contracts did not get tired. People did.

The next morning she emailed Ms. Harper, who ran the mock trial club, and asked whether the club might do a case about a phone company. She attached the contract, all twelve pages, and highlighted the sentence in yellow. Then she opened her own copy and read it once more, slowly, her finger tracking the line on the screen.

"Per applicable term," she said out loud, to the empty kitchen. "Which term."

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Most news articles use the 'inverted pyramid': the most important facts come first and less important details follow, so the opening paragraph carries the core story.
story:
I am excellent under pressure, which is why I had left the article until closing time on the night before the oral. The article was in Portuguese, a language I had been studying for exactly eleven weeks, and it was about a flood in some town whose name began with four consonants I could not pronounce. I spread it on the counter of my mother's restaurant, between the soy sauce and the tip jar, and began, sensibly, at the end.

The last paragraph was a nightmare of subjunctives. It mentioned a man named after a bird and a bridge that may or may not have been closed since Tuesday, and I worked through it word by word with my phone open to a dictionary, feeling extremely diligent and extremely doomed. At the far table Everett was stacking chairs upside down on tables, which was his whole contribution to the evening, and Misha was wiping the counter in slow circles while reading my face like weather.

"You've been on that same paragraph for twenty minutes," Misha said. "Your eye is twitching."

"It's not twitching. It's concentrating."

"It's twitching. I can hear it."

Everett drifted over, still holding a chair, because Everett never missed a chance to be right about something. He read over my shoulder for ten seconds, then tapped the top of the page. "Why are you starting at the bottom?"

"Because the bottom is where they put the conclusion. Obviously. Like an essay."

"It's not an essay, it's news." He said it with the smugness of someone whose uncle was a sportswriter, which he had told us roughly forty times. "Most news articles use the inverted pyramid. The most important facts come first, the less important details follow. The whole core story is in the opening paragraph."

"That's a stupid way to write," I said, but my heart had begun to palpitate in a way that was half dread and half the good kind, the kind you get when a locked door turns out to have been unlocked the whole time. I put my finger on the first paragraph and started over.

The first paragraph was a gift. Flood, town, two hundred people evacuated, shelter in a school. Four sentences, maybe thirty words I actually knew, and underneath them a shape I could feel: if I could say those four sentences out loud, in my terrible accent, I would have summarized the thing. The man named after a bird was, it turned out, quoted in paragraph five saying something petulant about the mayor, and the bridge was in the very last line, and neither of them mattered at all. I had spent twenty minutes on the trim and skipped the roof.

Then Mr. Fischer came in. He came in every Thursday at nine for takeout, and he taught media studies at the college, and I am ashamed to say I had been avoiding him for a week because he had offered to help me practice and I had said, with great confidence, "I have a system." Mr. Fischer ordered his usual and then noticed the article flattened under my elbow like a crime scene.

"How's the system?" he asked.

"Refined," I said. "Recently."

Misha snorted into the rag. Everett said, "She was reading it backwards," and I kicked him under the counter, or meant to, and got the leg of the stool instead, which hurt me more than it hurt him.

"Summarize it for me right now," Mr. Fischer said, and because the register was printing his receipt and my mother was in the kitchen and the exam was in fourteen hours, there was no graceful escape. I stood up straight behind the counter like a waitress presenting the specials. My Portuguese came out mangled but complete: flood, town, evacuations, school. It took me under a minute. Mr. Fischer nodded once, which from him was applause.

"And the bridge?" he asked, because of course he had read the article over my shoulder, because adults are like this.

"The bridge," I said, "is at the bottom of the pyramid, where it belongs."

He paid, took his bag, and paused at the door. "Tomorrow, start at the top," he said, which was a joke he had no right to make since I had figured that out myself, more or less, with assists. The door chimed behind him. Misha flipped the closed sign, and Everett began wiping the counter in the same slow circles she had abandoned, humming the little tune he always hummed, the one that had become the leitmotif of every late shift in that restaurant, though I could not have told you when that started.

I folded the article along its honest lines, first paragraph on the outside. Then Misha said, "Say it again, the whole thing, and this time don't smile in the middle like you got away with something," so I took a breath and began with the flood.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The area between two curves is found by integrating the upper function minus the lower function over the interval where they are ordered that way.
story:
Henry arrived at the community centre early, before the math club had even unlocked the room, and stood in the hallway eating the second half of a granola bar. Ms. Ferreira came down the corridor with a ring of keys and a stack of photocopies.

"You're the first one," she said. "You can put the desks in a circle."

He dragged six desks into something like a circle. On the board, in his own handwriting, was last week's problem, the one he had copied down and taken home: find the area between the line y equals x plus two and the parabola y equals x squared. He had worked on it for three nights, filling the margins of his history notes, and he had an answer, 4.5, which he liked because it was clean.

Maxym showed up with Calla, both of them arguing about a movie, and then Ms. Ferreira wrote the same two equations on the board and said, "All right, between these two curves, from where they cross to where they cross again. Go."

The room went quiet except for pencils. Henry watched Maxym work, because Maxym worked fast and usually got there first, and when Maxym leaned back and announced "Nine halves," Henry felt something open up in his chest. Nine halves was 4.5. The same answer.

"I got 4.5 too," Henry said, and Maxym gave him a thumbs up, and then Calla said, quietly, without looking up, "I got negative 4.5."

"Then you dropped a sign," Maxym said.

"I didn't." She turned her notebook around so they could see. Her work was tidier than either of theirs, each step boxed. She had integrated x squared minus the quantity x plus two, all of it, from minus one to two. Maxym had integrated the line minus the parabola. Same interval, same crossing points, opposite signs.

Ms. Ferreira was at the window watering a spider plant that did not need watering. Henry knew her rule about this, which was that she would not settle an argument until the room had genuinely tried to settle it itself. He also knew she was listening.

Maxym drew his setup on the board next to Calla's. "The line's on top," he said, tapping the sketch. "Look, between the crossing points, the line is above the parabola the whole way."

"So?" Calla said.

"So area can't be negative," Maxym said. "That's the whole point of area."

Henry had been about to say the same thing, and the fact that he stopped himself surprised him. He sat back down. It wasn't that Calla was right and Maxym was wrong, exactly. It was that the two of them had done the same mechanical thing in opposite directions, and the machinery itself didn't know which function was supposed to count as top. The machinery just subtracted whatever you told it to subtract. He found himself wanting to introspect on why he had never noticed that before, why he had treated integration like a vending machine, and then he decided that was a waste of a good Thursday and got up instead.

"Show me where you subtracted," he said to Calla, and she pointed. Then he took the marker from Maxym and wrote a third version, hers with the order flipped, and underneath it, the sentence he had never actually written down in three nights of homework: the area between two curves comes from integrating the upper function minus the lower function over the interval where they're ordered that way. "Upper minus lower," he said out loud, mostly to the board. "Not just any order. Upper minus lower, on the stretch where it actually is the upper one."

"Which is why I'm right," Maxym said.

"Which is why your number is right," Calla said. "My setup was still a real calculation. It just measured it upside down." She looked at her page. "Minus 4.5 is the same area with the sign flipped."

Ms. Ferreira set down the watering can. "Henry, what's the veracity of that claim, that Maxym's is the area and Calla's isn't?"

Henry thought about it. "They're both true calculations," he said. "One of them is the answer to the question we were asked. The other one is the answer to a question nobody asked, backwards." He paused. "But if the parabola were on top somewhere else, we'd have to split it up. Upper minus lower only works where that's actually the order. We checked between the crossing points, and it holds the whole way through here, but I only know that because we looked at the picture."

Ms. Ferreira was effusive in a way she almost never allowed herself, saying it was the best five minutes the club had had all year, and Maxym took a bow, and Calla rolled her eyes and started erasing the board, and Henry wrote upper minus lower in the margin of his notebook, twice, and then underlined the interval where they're ordered that way, because that was the part he had skipped for three nights, and he suspected it was the part that would bite him on the exam.

He capped the marker and handed it back to Maxym.

"Same time next week?" Maxym said.

"Same time," Henry said, and put his notebook in his bag with the granola bar wrapper still on the desk.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: By the JavaBeans naming convention, a getter for a field named 'score' is called getScore(), and a getter for a boolean field is usually named with 'is', like isActive().
story:
The basement smelled like dryer sheets and old carpet, and Abigail had claimed the only chair with a back while Nika sat cross-legged on the floor beside a laptop that hummed like it was thinking about retirement. On the screen was Mr. Lavoie's assignment sheet, which Abigail had read four times, and her own half-built Java class, which she had read even more times. The class was supposed to be simple. Private fields, getter methods, a test. Sixty marks, due Monday, and she had promised her mother she would stop treating computer science like a foreign language she could refuse to learn.

"Private means nobody can touch it," Nika said, chewing a pen cap. "That's the whole point, right? Like a locked box."

"Then why does it need getters at all," Abigail said, not quite a question, more of an accusation aimed at the ceiling of the subterranean room, where pipes ran overhead in orderly gray lines. She typed the fields first: an int called score, a boolean called active. That part she could do. It was the methods that had her cornered.

Ariane arrived at seven with her own laptop and a grievance. She dropped onto the couch, kicked a pillow onto the floor, and opened a file called FINAL_v3_REALLY.java. "My teammate," she announced, "is a menace. Every getter he wrote is named differently. One of them is giveValue. One is fetchScore. One is just the letter g." She turned the screen so they could see, and Abigail leaned over and saw that it was all true, a scavenger hunt of methods with no logic to them, unless the logic was spite.

"There's a convention," Abigail said slowly, because she was only half sure, only remembering a slide Mr. Lavoie had flashed for four seconds before moving on to encapsulation. "For a field named score, the getter is called getScore. Capital S." She paused. "And for a boolean, it's different. A boolean field named active would be isActive. With the is."

Ariane stared at her. "How do you know that?"

"I don't know how I know that. It's like the password screen on an old phone. My hands remember, not my brain." Abigail pulled the assignment back up and began to type, and for once the words came out in the right shapes: public int getScore(), public boolean isActive(). She sat back. "So your teammate's code is bad not just because it's ugly. It's bad because it's not what anyone expects. Anyone reading it has to guess."

From the floor, Nika watched this happen with the mild fascination of someone watching a friend assemble furniture without the instructions. Abigail was not, in Nika's private assessment, a natural at this. She was a person who argued with inanimate objects and won roughly half the time. But there was something happening now that Nika had seen before, in the chemistry unit, in the driving lessons. Abigail went quiet, and then she went stubborn, and then she went right. She was not a sycophant about any of it; she never flattered the machine or the mark scheme the way some students did, cooing at rubrics as though grades were handed out for enthusiasm. She just worked, jaw set, deleting whole lines without ceremony.

"What's the test supposed to prove?" Nika asked.

"That the box actually works. That I can put a score in and get the same score out." Abigail wrote a small test method, set the score to ninety, and printed what came back. She ran it. Nothing happened, which was its own kind of message. She read the console twice, cogitated with her chin in her hand, and found the missing semicolon hiding at the end of line thirty-one like a spider behind a bookshelf. She added it and ran the program again.

Ninety.

"Say it louder," Ariane said.

"Ninety," Abigail said, louder, and then, quieter, "but I still don't get why the fields have to be private if we're just going to hand the values out through getters anyway. Seems like a lot of ceremony for a door."

Ariane had stopped listening somewhere around the second semicolon. She was renaming her teammate's getters one by one, muttering fetchScore into the void as she deleted it, and the file was shrinking toward something a person could actually read. "He's going to merge over all this," she said. "He's going to be furious."

"Good," said Nika.

Abigail saved her work, then saved it again to a second place, a habit her father had taught her after the great laptop collapse of the previous spring. She looked at the class on the screen, score and active behind their private wall, getScore and isActive standing politely outside it, the test at the bottom proving the whole arrangement to whoever cared to look. She was still not certain she understood the philosophy of it. She was certain the program ran. On Monday Mr. Lavoie would either nod or he wouldn't, and she had decided she could survive both outcomes, though she preferred one.

Ariane closed her laptop. "GetScore," she said to the ceiling. "Just getScore. Was that so hard."

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In 1868 the Senate acquitted President Andrew Johnson by one vote: 35 senators voted to convict, one short of the two-thirds needed.
story:
Maya had told herself, on the walk to the library, that she would be finished with the essay in two hours, and this was the first thing she got wrong. The assignment was Mr. Schneider's: compare how a parliamentary system and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government, and she had assumed the hard part would be the choosing. Prime ministers, she had learned, could be swapped out by a vote of no confidence, sometimes in a single afternoon, the way Cedrick swapped girlfriends. Presidents had terms. Presidents had elections. That much she was sure of, or sure enough to have written half a page already.

The removal part was where the afternoon went. She had spread three books and her notebook across the table by the window, where the late light made the paper look warm and important, and Tenzin had appeared beside her with a stack of manga he claimed were for "research." He was, everyone agreed, the library's resident raconteur, and she should have known that letting him sit down would cost her forty minutes on the subject of his uncle's wedding.

"You're still on this?" Tenzin said finally, peering over her shoulder. "Just write that presidents are basically kings for four years."

"They're not kings." She pulled the notebook back. "There's impeachment."

"Which never works."

"It works." She paused. "It worked once. Almost." She flipped through the book she'd been reading, the one with the cracked spine, because she remembered a number she'd seen and wanted to see it again. There it was. "In 1868 the Senate acquitted President Andrew Johnson by one vote. Thirty-five senators voted to convict, one short of the two-thirds they needed."

Tenzin leaned in, actually interested for once. "One vote? One guy somewhere decided the president stays?"

"One vote short," she said. "Thirty-five to convict, and they needed thirty-six." She did the arithmetic twice on her fingers, because she distrusted her own arithmetic more than she distrusted the book.

The number mesmerized her for the rest of the hour, in a way she could not quite justify to herself. She kept circling back to it. In a parliamentary system, the book said, a prime minister fell when the parliament withdrew its confidence, which was a knife always on the table. In the presidential system the knife was locked in a box, and the box needed two-thirds of the Senate, and in 1868 the box had stayed shut by a single vote. She wrote, then crossed out, then wrote again: which system is more afraid of instability, and which more afraid of a leader who cannot be removed?

Cedrick arrived at four with a smoothie and strong opinions. "One vote is obviously too thin," he said, straw between his teeth. "Imagine being one senator. Imagine having that on you."

"But flip it," Maya said. "Maybe one vote is exactly the point. The bar is so high that removing a president is supposed to be nearly impossible, so the vote isn't thin, it's the design working." She heard herself say it and believed it about seventy percent, which was more than she believed most of what she said.

"That's a virulent take," Cedrick said.

"That's not what virulent means."

"It means strong."

"It means poisonous. Like a virus." She was enjoying this more than the essay. "Use intense."

Tenzin raised his manga like a shield. "Both systems get rid of bad leaders eventually. One just does it with a shrug and the other with a trial that fails by one vote. Write that."

By six the light had gone flat and the librarian was pushing a cart of returns past their table, its wheels squeaking in that particular library way, apologetic and unfixable. Maya had two pages, a decent argument, and a sentence at the bottom she had not shown the others: that she couldn't decide whether the near-impossibility of removing a president was wisdom or stubbornness, and that maybe the honest answer was that the 1868 vote had been one senator's conscience or cowardice, and no system could tell you which. She would probably delete that sentence before handing it in. Or maybe not.

"Done?" Cedrick asked, collecting his cup.

"Done enough." She closed the book with the cracked spine and slid it toward the returns pile at the end of the shelf, the way she'd seen other people do it, and stood there a second with her hand on the cover.

"One vote," Tenzin said from the door, holding it open. "Thirty-five to thirty-six."

"Thirty-five to convict," Maya said. "Get it right."

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: MLA style cites sources in the text with the author's name and page number in parentheses, and lists the full sources at the end under the heading 'Works Cited'.
story:
The bell over the cafe door rang twice before Sadie noticed it, because she was counting the quotation marks in her draft. She had a table near the window, a cold hot chocolate, and a history paper due Friday that Mr. Gill had handed back with one red circle on the last page. The circle was around her heading, which said Works Cited. Beside it he had written, in his blunt handwriting, see me.

Rosemarie dropped into the chair opposite her, peeling off her scarf. "You look pugnacious," she said. "Like the paper insulted your family."

"It sort of did." Sadie turned the page around. "He circled Works Cited like it's a crime. That's what Ms. Ahlgren wanted all year in English. Parentheses with the author's name and the page number, and then the full sources listed at the end under Works Cited. I finally got good at it. Now it's wrong?"

Rosemarie pulled the paper closer and studied it the way she studied menus, with her chin in her hand. "My brother says history teachers want footnotes. Little numbers, notes at the bottom of the page." She said this with authority, though her brother had failed geography. "And he says they call the list at the end a bibliography."

"A bibliography." Sadie said the word slowly, the way you'd test a plank across a stream. "Not Works Cited."

"Rosemarie!" A voice from the counter, where Clemence stood holding two coffees she refused to carry alone. She had a job interview at the cafe on Saturday and had decided to practice being an employee, which so far meant criticizing the actual employees. "They put the foam on wrong. Look at it. Look."

Sadie looked. The foam looked like foam. But Clemence wanted to be indignant on someone's behalf, possibly the coffee's, and there was no stopping her until she had been agreed with. "Tragic," Sadie said, and Clemence nodded once, satisfied, and carried the cups to a table by the poetry shelf.

Rosemarie turned the paper back around. "So why does it matter? The sources are the same sources."

"That's what I asked myself." Sadie had spent the walk to the cafe trying not to introspect about it and failing, because the question kept opening under her like a trapdoor. She had been proud of that heading. In September she couldn't do any of it; she'd cited a website by pasting the whole URL into the middle of a sentence, and Ms. Ahlgren had read it aloud to herself with her lips moving. By June, Sadie could put the author's name and the page number in parentheses and build the Works Cited list underneath, and it looked like something a real person wrote. Now she was in Mr. Gill's class, in that strange stretch between summer and whatever came after, and the ground rules had changed without telling her.

"He gave me a sample paper," she said, pulling it from her folder. It belonged to some former student, photocopied, with little numbers scattered through the sentences like bird tracks. At the bottom of each page, a row of notes. At the end, the heading, plain as anything: Bibliography. "So that's the system he wants. Name, title, publisher, and the note numbers instead of the parentheses."

"Then just do that," Rosemarie said. "Copy the system."

"It's not that simple." Sadie slid the sample toward her. "Look at the third page. He wrote nice use of the source but what do you argue. All year in English I was learning where the commas go. Nobody asked me if I believed anything."

Clemence appeared again, mug-less, having finished her audit of the counter. "I'm going to tell them Saturday that I have customer service experience," she announced. "Because I do. In spirit."

"You have never served a customer," Rosemarie said.

"I've been a customer. It's the same field." Clemence stole a corner of Sadie's muffin and retreated to defend the sugar station.

Sadie laughed, and then stopped, because she was looking at the red circle again. Last spring, when she'd had to drop out of the debate team, the coach had told her she argued like a card catalogue, all entries and no verdict. It had stung, mostly because it was accurate. She had spent a year learning to file knowledge and none learning to take a side.

Rosemarie was watching her. "You're doing the face."

"I think the heading isn't the real problem. I can fix the heading in ten minutes. MLA wants the name and page number in parentheses and the list at the end under Works Cited, and I already know that; now I just have to learn his way instead." She flattened the draft against the table. "The problem is the question he wrote. What do I argue. I don't know yet. I've been quoting people for so long I forgot the sources were supposed to add up to something."

Rosemarie considered this, chin in hand again. "So argue something small. Argue that the railway thing was mostly about money. My brother says everything is mostly about money."

"My paper's about shipwrecks."

"Then argue something about ships."

Sadie took out a pen, crossed out Works Cited, and wrote Bibliography above it, carefully, in ink. Then she turned to the first page and wrote, in the margin, next to the nice use of the source comment, a single question mark. Below it, after a pause, she wrote the words: I think.

"Good start," Rosemarie said, stealing the pen.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: Ireland's Great Famine began in 1845 when potato blight struck a population that relied heavily on one potato variety, the Lumper, whose lack of genetic variety left it vulnerable.
story:
The folding chairs in the council chamber were colder than Isabelle expected, metal rungs pressing through her jeans as she sat with her notes collated into one stapled packet, edges squared like something that mattered. She had spent three evenings in the library database and one afternoon at the community garden on Halstead Street, where the soil test results were taped to the shed window and where Mr. Ferreira, who had run the garden for eleven years, wanted to tear out the mixed plots and plant the whole half-acre in a single high-yield squash. Tonight the council would vote on whether the garden could keep its water tap, and Mr. Ferreira had asked her, the youngest volunteer, to speak in favor of his plan. More food, he said. Fewer arguments about who gets which bed.

Abbigail sat beside her, chewing the end of a pen. "You're going to tell them about the potatoes," she whispered. Beckham, on her other side, leaned past her. "Which potatoes?"

"The Irish ones," Abbigail said. "She's been talking about them for a week."

Isabelle had found it by accident, chasing a citation about crop yields, and it had unsettled her more than she could initially account for. Ireland's Great Famine began in 1845 when potato blight struck a population that relied heavily on one potato variety, the Lumper, whose lack of genetic variety left it vulnerable. One variety. She had read the sentence four times, then copied it onto an index card and carried it to school in her back pocket until the corners went soft. At the dinner table she had tried to explain it to her mother, who worked nights at the hospital and fell asleep over her tea, and to her father, who said that people starve in famines for political reasons too, and that blaming a potato was too simple. Both things could be true, Isabelle had thought, and neither canceled the other.

Ms. Bouchard, the clerk, called the agenda item, and the chamber smelled of burnt coffee and floor wax, the overhead lights buzzing at a pitch that made her teeth ache. A woman from the development office spoke first, crisp and unbothered, explaining that the garden's lot had been appraised and that a proposed affordable housing project would take its place unless the garden could demonstrate, in her phrase, "material community benefit." The water tap was a rounding error, she implied; the land was the real question. Behind Isabelle, someone's chair scraped. Mr. Ferreira stood, laid out his squash plan with a laminated chart, and mentioned the food bank twice. His hands were steady. His chart had a bar graph.

When Ms. Bouchard called for public comment, Isabelle stood before she felt ready, and her voice came out thin in the microphone. "I'm a volunteer at the garden," she said. "I want to say something about the planting plan, and then something about the land." She told them about the Lumper, about 1845, about the blight, and she felt the room shift, the specific quiet of people listening. "A whole country leaned on one potato," she said, "and when the blight came, there wasn't anything standing between the people and hunger. Our garden has thirty-one crops. If one fails, the others hold." She said she wasn't against the squash, that hungry people this winter mattered more than an abstraction, but that the garden's mixed beds were not an ornament. They were the part that lasted.

Then she turned to the land, and this was where her prepared remarks ended and something less certain began. She said the housing project and the garden were being presented as rivals when the actual conflict was between two needs the city had refused to fund at once, that the deleterious choice would be pretending the vote itself solved anything. "I don't know what the right answer is," she said, and heard Abbigail's pen stop. "I know what the wrong process looks like. It looks like this." She sat down with her ears burning.

A council member, the one with the reading glasses, asked whether the garden had considered a single reliable crop, given the food bank's demand. Isabelle said the Lumper had been reliable too, until it wasn't. Beckham, unexpectedly, stood and spoke for ninety seconds about the after-school plots, his voice cracking once, his hands shaking, and she understood he had been planning this without telling either of them.

The twist came from Ms. Bouchard, quiet and procedural. Reading from a memorandum, she noted that the housing proposal, as submitted, contained no units priced for families like those on the garden's waiting list, because the subsidy program had been suspended the previous spring. The development office's woman went still. The appraisal assumed a market-rate building on land the garden had improved for a decade, its compost built by volunteers, its tap paid for by a bake sale Isabelle herself had organized in seventh grade. The garden had raised the value of the lot, and the lot was now being taken because of that value. Consanguinity, Abbigail whispered, was the wrong word for it but the right feeling: the two things were related by blood and pretending otherwise.

The council deferred the vote to next month. Outside, under the sodium lights, Mr. Ferreira found her by the bike rack. "You didn't argue for my chart," he said. He didn't sound angry. He sounded like a man rechecking his arithmetic. "Thirty-one crops," he repeated. "You counted them."

"On Tuesday," Isabelle said. "I counted on Tuesday."

He looked at the garden gate down the street, at the frost already silvering the fence wire, and pulled his laminated chart out from under his arm, creasing it slowly in half.

"Come by Saturday," he said. "We'll figure out what to plant where."

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: In common-law jurisdictions, including most of the US, a contract made by a minor is generally voidable by the minor, with exceptions such as contracts for necessities.
story:
The fluorescent light above the rental counter made everything look already regretted, the laminate scuffed in gray crescents, the pens chained to their little wooden blocks. Isabelle stood in line behind a man in a rain-dark coat and rehearsed what she would say, because the interview at Wellesley was at two o'clock and her mother was still on a tarmac in Charlotte, texting her apologies in fragments. The reservation was in her mother's name. The car, a silver sedan with a full tank and nobody to claim it, sat somewhere in the garage behind the counter, and Isabelle had three hours and a driver's license that said she was seventeen.

"I can take it," she said when she reached the agent, sliding the confirmation email across the counter. "It's paid for. She's my mom. I'm on the insurance."

The agent, a woman with reading glasses pushed up into her hair, looked at the screen, then at Isabelle, then at the license. "Renter has to sign the agreement in person. And our policy is twenty-one minimum, twenty-five to avoid the young-driver fee."

"I've been driving since I was fifteen."

"That's not something I can adjust."

Isabelle had prepared for this, or believed she had. She had printed the insurance card, the itinerary, the email. She had even prognosticated, on the drive from school to the airport, exactly how the conversation would go, and in her imagination the agent had been moved by the weltschmerz of it all, by the sheer unfairness of a delayed mother and a two o'clock appointment. The actual agent was neither cruel nor kind. She was simply the counter, and the counter was a synecdoche for everything else: terms, conditions, initials required in every small box, the whole apparatus that treated her as a signature she could not yet legally give.

It had been different in September, and she hadn't appreciated it then. She and Caiden had stood at the gym's front desk with a special student rate folded in his hand, and the clerk had said, without drama, that at seventeen his membership contract needed a parent's signature. Caiden had been morose about it for a week, slouching through lunch, saying the gym just didn't want teenagers. But Mr. Farah-Ali, when Isabelle mentioned it after class, had said only one thing before turning back to his grading: "A contract made by a minor is generally voidable by the minor. Common law. Most of the US. There are exceptions, contracts for necessities, but a gym membership isn't one." He said it the way he said most things, as though handing her something fragile to carry.

She had carried it. In October she had used it, quietly, when the photography studio in the next town refused to return her deposit on a package she'd signed for herself, a senior-portrait contract with a cancellation clause she hadn't read. She had written a letter, careful and formal, citing exactly what Mr. Farah-Ali had said, and the deposit had come back in ten days with no note. Caiden had called it a superpower. She hadn't corrected him, but she remembered standing at the mailbox feeling less powerful than lucky, and a little dishonest, as if she'd found a loophole in herself.

Now, at the counter, the fact turned around and faced her. Voidable by the minor. Not voidable for her. The rule that had returned her deposit was the same rule that kept the keys on the agent's side of the laminate. She could not even argue that her mother had consented, because consent was not hers to give on someone else's contract, and she understood, with a clarity that stung, that the law she'd wielded was not a weapon on her side. It was a wall with two faces.

"Can my mom sign over the phone?" she asked. "Or add me as an authorized driver remotely? She's landing in an hour, maybe less."

The agent typed something, paused, typed again. Behind Isabelle, the man in the rain coat shifted his weight, and somewhere in the garage a horn sounded twice, short and impatient. "I can put a note on the reservation," the agent said. "If she's landed and can verify by the time you're through security again, the counter at the terminal can process it. That's the best I can do. You'd still need her there for the signature."

"An hour," Isabelle said. "The interview's at two."

"You could call the school."

She looked at the email on her phone, the itineraries, the confirmation number, all the paper she had believed was proof of something. Behind her, Caiden's voice from lunch in October, laughing: so you can just break any deal you want until you're eighteen? And her answer, which she had thought was a joke: basically, unless it's something I actually need. She hadn't thought about what counted as needing. A ride to an interview was probably a necessity, but not in the way the law meant it, and she could not make the law mean what she wanted it to mean. That was the part Caiden hadn't asked about, and the part she hadn't wanted to explain.

She called the admissions office while the agent printed a copy of the reservation for the terminal desk. The phone was warm against her ear and a recorded voice offered her options in a pleasant, unhurried cadence. When a real person finally answered, a woman who sounded younger than her mother, Isabelle said, "Hi, my name is Isabelle. I have a two o'clock interview and my flight, my mother's flight, is delayed." She said it evenly, without prognosticating, and listened to the pause on the line while somewhere behind her the agent set a set of keys, not hers, on the counter with a small bright sound.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude, about 95 degrees Celsius at 5,000 feet, so boiled foods take longer to cook.
story:
The pasta in Jasmine's pot had been boiling for eleven minutes, and it was still hard in the middle. She fished out a piece, blew on it, and bit down on something that felt like a pencil eraser with ambitions.

"Timer's right," Ada said, holding up her phone as evidence, as though the phone might be called to testify. "Box says ten minutes. We did eleven. That's extra."

"Extra isn't always enough," Jasmine said, which was the kind of thing her grandmother used to say about forgiveness, but which she now applied to elbow macaroni.

They were in the cooking classroom at the end of the hall, the one with six stovetops and a wall of dented pots, and Mr. Whitaker had assigned each pair a dish for the family-dinner unit. Jasmine and Ada had drawn pasta with tomato sauce, which Ada called "the participation trophy of recipes" and which Jasmine had secretly been glad about, because her mother was working the late shift and her little brother would eat almost anything if it was orange. It was supposed to be simple. It was not being simple.

Martin leaned over from the next station, where his roux was going the color of weak tea. "Mine did that last week," he said. "I boiled potatoes for the mash forever and they crunched. I thought I was losing my mind."

"You were already losing it," Ada said. "But go on."

Jasmine stared into the pot. The water was rolling hard, furious bubbles crashing against the macaroni, and yet the pasta sat there, stubborn. Something nudged at her, a memory from the summer, the family campsite above the tree line where the pasta had also come out hard and her father had stood over the stove saying, "That's not possible, I've made pasta a thousand times." She had looked it up then, on one bar of signal, and the answer had seemed like trivia. Now it felt personal. At high altitude, water boils at a lower temperature, about 95 degrees Celsius at 5,000 feet, so boiled foods take longer to cook. And their town, she was fairly sure, sat right around 5,000 feet. The water wasn't lying to her. It was just doing the best it could under the circumstances, which was a slightly cooler best, and slightly cooler water needed more time.

"Ada," she said slowly, "where's the school? Elevation-wise."

Ada typed with the speed of someone who had settled many arguments this way. "Four thousand nine hundred feet. Why, are we going to blame the mountain?"

"We're going to blame the mountain," Jasmine said, and felt a small, unreasonable triumph, the visceral satisfaction of a mystery cracking open. "Water boils cooler up here. Ninety-five degrees at five thousand feet. So everything takes longer. It's not us. It's geography."

Martin pointed a wooden spoon at her like a scepter. "The potatoes. I knew it. I want a formal apology from this entire town."

"You'll want a long time," Mr. Whitaker said, drifting past with the mild rectitude of a man who had watched three decades of students blame their tools. "You'll get a longer apology than you expected."

Jasmine reset the timer for six more minutes, then, after a moment of honest doubt, added two on top of that, because the internet had been vague and the altitude was approximate and she was guessing, really, at the border between enough and mush. Ada stirred the sauce. Martin's roux finally thickened and he celebrated so loudly that the group making frittatas turned around, which he took as applause.

While the pasta softened, Jasmine thought about calling her father to tell him the campsite pasta hadn't been his fault, and decided she would, but not in a way that sounded like a lecture. Maybe just, "We figured out the pasta thing." Let him ask. She also thought about how strange it was that the same fact could be trivia in July and urgent in November, that knowing a thing and knowing when to use it were different skills entirely, and that she couldn't fully explain how she'd chosen eight minutes over six, only that she'd weighed the evidence and jumped. She was okay with the jump. She would taste the pasta and find out.

At minute eight she pulled a piece, bit it, and held up a finger for silence while she chewed. Then she grinned and drained the pot, steam billowing up toward the vent fan, the sauce already bubbling on the back burner.

"Tell the mountain," Ada announced to the whole room, "that we won."

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: The Common European Framework of Reference describes a B2 speaker as able to explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options.
story:
Charlie had claimed the sunroom at her grandmother's house because it was the only room where nobody watched television, and for three afternoons she had sat there with her German notes spread across the wicker table, trying to argue about city car bans in a language she had been studying for four years. The assignment sheet from her course, photocopied and creased, specified five minutes on a topical issue, delivered entirely in German, and at the bottom her teacher had written "B2" in green ink. Charlie had looked it up on her phone in the kitchen while her grandmother sliced apples: the Common European Framework of Reference described a B2 speaker as able to explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options. She read the sentence twice. It calmed her and then irritated her, because it meant the task was not really about winning. It was about holding more than one side at once, in a language that kept dissolving on her.

She practiced in the garden where the bees argued with the lavender. Meghan had sent a scathing voice message the night before, mocking the whole exercise: five minutes of fake debating in a class where nobody actually disagreed. "You'll say cars are bad but also convenient, and everyone will nod, and Herr somebody will give you a four." Meghan wanted Charlie to pick something that wouldproblematize the format itself, to argue so strangely that the teacher would have to respond. Charlie had laughed at the time, lying on her bed with the phone on her stomach, but now, pacing the flagstones and repeating "einerseits, andererseits" until the words lost their edges, she wondered whether Meghan's bravado was just a different kind of hiding. At least Charlie was attempting the thing. At least she was here, in her grandmother's garden, saying clumsy sentences to the bees.

The topic she had chosen was whether old buildings should be demolished for new housing, which had seemed safely abstract until she remembered that her grandmother's own street had lost two houses to a developer the year before. Her grandmother, Oma, had lived in this house for fifty-one years, had raised Charlie's mother in the room that now held the sewing machine, and had watched the corner house come down in a single loud morning. Charlie had not been there. She had been at school, and when she called that evening her grandmother had said only, "Es ist weg," it is gone, and changed the subject to whether Charlie was eating enough.

In the sunroom on the fourth afternoon, Charlie laid out her notes in two columns, Vorteile on the left, Nachteile on the right, and tried to speak for five minutes without stopping. She got to ninety seconds before the grammar failed her. She got to two minutes before the argument failed her, because the honest version kept collapsing: new housing was necessary, and old buildings were irreplaceable, and both claims were true, and the framework, as far as she could tell, did not care which one she believed. It only wanted her to show the scales. She felt this as a small betrayal of something she could not name, a suspicion that balanced views were a kind of casuistry, a clever weighing that let you off the hook of choosing. Then she thought of her grandmother saying "es ist weg" and could not decide whether the weighing was cowardice or respect.

Her grandmother came in with tea and sat down without asking, which she never did, and Charlie, flustered, covered her notes with her forearm.

"Was ist das?" her grandmother asked, nodding at the hidden page, and Charlie, before she could decide against it, answered in German, slowly: "I am learning to debate. To explain a viewpoint, with the advantages and disadvantages of different options. For my level. B2." The sentence came out whole, unbroken, the longest thing she had ever said in the language without rehearsing it, and her grandmother set down the teapot.

"You will debate the houses," her grandmother said. Not a question. She had seen the topic line, of course, weeks ago perhaps, over Charlie's shoulder, in the kitchen. Charlie waited for her to object, to say it was too close, to ask her to choose the cars instead. Instead her grandmother folded her hands and said, in English, "Then say both sides to me. I am your class."

So Charlie stood in the sunroom, sweat cooling on her back, and began. She said that cities needed homes for young families, that rents were cruel, that demolition was sometimes honest. She said that a street was a kind of memory that could not be rebuilt, that her grandmother had watched a house vanish in one morning, and here her voice shook but her German did not, because she had practiced the hard vowels all week and the sentences arrived like they had been waiting. She gave examples. She gave counterexamples. Somewhere in the fourth minute she stopped performing balance and started thinking out loud, saying that maybe the framework was right, maybe the discipline of holding both sides was itself the skill, and maybe it was also a way of never standing anywhere. She said she did not know. "Ich weiss es nicht," she said, and it was the easiest sentence of the five minutes.

When she finished, her grandmother was looking at the window, not at her. "The corner house," she said at last, "the developer sent a letter. Last week. They want this one also." Charlie sat down slowly on the wicker stool, all her columns suddenly weightless. "What did you write back?" she asked, and her grandmother smiled in a way that Charlie had never seen before, somewhere between grief and a dare, and said, "Nothing yet. Say my side for me. You have the practice now."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: The standard tuning note is A above middle C at 440 hertz, formalized by the International Organization for Standardization as ISO 16.
story:
Alexandra had been studying oboe with Mr. He for six weeks, and in that time she had broken one reed, two resolutions, and, according to Chiara, the record for the longest note ever held in the stairwell of the community center, which Chiara had timed at forty-one seconds out of pure spite. The spite was affectionate. Mostly. On the Thursday before the first rehearsal of the center's summer band, Mr. He handed her the battered leather case that held his tuning fork and said, "You give the A tonight. You're ready."

The band tuned before every rehearsal, and the A came from the oboe, which meant that whatever came out of Alexandra's reed became true for thirty people at once. She had liked the sound of that, the small empire of it, until she was actually standing in front of them with Chantelle grinning at her from the second clarinet row and Chiara photographing the moment for posterity. Mr. He held up his phone with a tuner app running, its needle trembling around a green line. "Standard concert pitch," he said. "A above middle C, four forty." He tapped the screen. "It's ISO 16, so it's official. The whole world agreed."

She took the breath, and the note wavered, palpitated really, like something small and alive that she was carrying in her cupped hands, and the needle slid flat and then sharp and then, for three seconds that felt like a public holiday, sat still on the green. Around her the band murmured into tune, a spreading ripple of A's, and Chantelle called out, "Sounded like a duck being rescued, but a duck in tune," and Alexandra laughed so hard she had to swallow the note before it turned vitriolic.

Afterward, in the parking lot, Chiara showed her the phone video, and Alexandra noticed something she hadn't heard live. Halfway through the tuning, when the brass came in, the pitch of the whole band sagged, a slow collective sinking, and then snapped back up. She watched it four times with her thumb over the pause button. "They're not flat," she said slowly. "Somebody in there is pulling the whole thing down, and everyone else is bending toward them."

The message came that night, from an unknown number, and Chiara forwarded it to the group chat with the caption WELL WELL WELL. It read: "To the oboe player. Your A was correct, 440, ISO 16 and everything, very impressive, very international. But I have played at 438 for thirty years because it sounds warmer, and I am not changing for an app. Tune me out. Sincerely, the bassoon." Alexandra read it aloud to her mother, twice, because the first time she couldn't get through the word "international" without her voice going strange. "He signed it," she said. "From the bassoon. Like the instrument wrote it."

She thought about the old man all through Friday. He wasn't wrong about warmth, exactly; she'd read forum threads where whole orchestras admitted to creeping upward, or clinging downward, like regional accents that never fully standardize. Standard pitch was a treaty, and like most treaties it held only as long as everyone pretended it was natural. She had always liked rules you could verify, the clean certainty of four forty, the needle on the green line, and she'd privately thought of players like the bassoonist as stubborn, a genotype of musician that refused to hybridize. But there was something in a man deciding, alone, for thirty years, that his ears outranked an international organization.

At Saturday's rehearsal she brought both truths to the stand. Before giving the A, she played it once, then bent it deliberately, warmly, down toward where the bassoon lived, and heard the low reeds settle around it like they'd been waiting. Then she straightened it back to 440, and the brass and strings rose to meet her. Two tunings, thirty seconds apart, and the whole band had gone along with it. Afterward the old bassoonist found her by the door. He did not introduce himself. He looked at his shoes and said, "The second one was better," and then, so quietly she almost missed it, "The first one was better too."

She started a reply to him that night, got as far as "Dear Bassoon," which made Chiara laugh so hard she had to leave the room, and then deleted it, because she still didn't know whether she agreed with herself about what she'd done. At the next rehearsal Mr. He handed her the phone again, needle waiting, green line patient as ever, and Alexandra lifted the reed to her lips and glanced, just once, toward the back row.

"Four forty," she said. "But I'll meet you halfway."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: The 1996 book Continuing Bonds, by Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman, argued that keeping a lasting connection with someone who has died is a normal part of grief, not a failure to move on.
story:
The hospital smelled like the floor wax they used in his middle school, and Landon kept noticing that instead of noticing anything about his grandfather, who was dead two floors above him. His mother had called at 6:40 in the morning, before his alarm, and he had lain still for a full minute with the phone against his ear, hearing her breathe in the parking garage. Then she had said the word, and he had gotten dressed.

He had skipped the Tuesday visit. That was the thing he could not stop sorting through on the elevator. There had been a calc test Thursday and a history paper Friday, and his grandfather had been the kind of man who said, "Study, don't sit here watching me watch television," so Landon had studied, and told himself his grandfather would have wanted it, and now the visit he had traded away was the last one there would ever be. He and his own excuse had a kind of complicity, he thought; neither had forced the other, but together they had gotten it done.

The room was on the fourth floor, in the wing where his grandfather had volunteered for eleven years after retiring from his practice, reading discharge papers aloud to patients who had no one to read them to. The hospital had put him there partly out of sentiment, the charge nurse told Landon's mother, and partly because the unit served a lot of indigent patients, people who came in through the emergency room and had no regular doctor, and the staff thought it would please him to be among them. He had died at 4:15 in the morning, in his sleep, with the television on mute.

Kinsley was in the family lounge when Landon came out of the room. She had driven forty minutes on a Saturday, which they would both pretend later was nothing. She sat with a paper cup of vending machine coffee and did not say she was sorry, which he was grateful for, and instead asked what the room had been like, and he told her about the muted television, still on, still tuned to the weather channel.

"Can I tell you something weird," she said. Not really a question. "After my grandma died, my sister gave me this book. Continuing Bonds. It came out in 1996, these three people wrote it, Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman, and Steven Nickman. Their whole argument was that keeping a connection with someone who died is a normal part of grief. Not a failure to move on." She turned the cup in her hands. "I used to talk to her while I cooked. Her recipes. I thought I was losing it, and the book said no, that's just what people do."

"So what, I'm supposed to feel better because some book says it's fine to keep him around?"

"I'm saying I've done it for two years and it hasn't killed me."

Abbey arrived then, out of breath from the stairwell because she claimed elevators made her dizzy, and she had a bag of clementines, which was a thing she did at funerals and hospitals and once at a track meet where Landon had pulled a hamstring. She sat down and started peeling one without asking if anyone wanted anything, and the sharp citrus smell cut through the coffee and the floor wax, and Landon realized he was hungry, and then felt obscurely guilty about being hungry, and then decided his grandfather would have found that funny, actually, would have said, "Eat, you're not doing him any good starving."

Later the three of them went down to the cafeteria, because his mother was still upstairs with the paperwork and had told him to be somewhere other than the hallway. In the line he understood that he was going to have to recalibrate some basic assumption, the one where grieving meant shrinking the person down until he fit into a compartment marked before. He did not want to shrink his grandfather. He wanted the volunteer badge and the terrible puns and the way the man pronounced "lobotomy" as though it were a threat to keep exactly their size, and he was going to have to work out how to live with a full-sized dead person, which Kinsley's book apparently said people did all the time, though he was not sure yet whether he believed a book could give him permission for anything.

Kinsley wanted something too, he could see it now, the way she kept almost speaking and then peeling another clementine section instead. Finally she said, "There's a thing Monday, the vigil thing at the hospice chapel, and I didn't go to my grandma's and I've regretted it for two years, and I don't want you to have the same thing. So come with me. You don't have to talk or pray or anything."

He looked at the tray in front of him, the sandwich he had taken without choosing. His grandfather had eaten in this cafeteria probably four hundred times, at this kind of table, with people who had no one. "Okay," Landon said. "Monday." Then he picked up the sandwich and took the first bite, and it tasted exactly the way hospital food is supposed to taste, and he ate all of it.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water, and kneading longer makes the gluten network stronger and the bread chewier.
story:
Morgan set the flour bin back on the shelf and looked at the loaf cooling on the rack, its crust dull where it should have shone, its middle sunken like a pillow someone had slept on wrong. Her mother had taken one slice at dinner, buttered it, and said nothing, which was worse than criticism because it left Morgan to imagine the verdict on her behalf. She could not stop thinking about it. Two weekends ago she had decided the family would eat real bread, bread she had made, and now the evidence sat on the counter, dense and crumbly, refusing to exculpate her from the charge of having rushed.

She tipped the loaf over and thumped the bottom. It sounded like a knock on a closed door. Kayne had told her at lunch, between bites of cafeteria pizza, that his grandmother in Guyana made bread every Sunday and never measured anything, and Morgan had wanted that kind of authority so badly she had half believed measuring was the problem. Mariane, who read everything, had gone the other way and sent her a chart of gram weights and hydration percentages, so precise it felt like a chemistry test. Between Kayne's feel and Mariane's numbers Morgan had chosen neither, exactly, and had ended with this door-knocking brick.

She got out the flour again. If she was going to fail, she wanted to fail while paying attention.

Her younger brother wandered in for a glass of milk and stayed to watch her tip flour into the bowl, add water, and stir until the shaggy mass held together. "What's that," he said, meaning the dough.

"Flour and water," Morgan said. "The proteins in flour, glutenin and gliadin, they mix with the water, and that's when gluten forms." She turned the dough out onto the counter. "Kneading it longer makes the gluten network stronger. And the bread chewier."

"So knead a lot."

"That's the theory."

She set the kitchen timer for eight minutes and began. The dough tore at first, then smoothed under her palms, and she thought about her grandmother, who had cooked in a milieu of gasoline stoves and borrowed kitchens and never once, as far as Morgan knew, weighed anything, and who had still somehow produced food people remembered after she was gone. Morgan had no such excuse. She had a stand mixer in the pantry she hadn't bothered to carry out. She had chosen hands because hands felt like proof of something, though she could not have said what, and she was honest enough with herself to admit the choice had been at least partly for the look of the thing.

When the timer rang she cut a small piece of dough and stretched it between her fingers until it thinned into a window, translucent at the center, and tore only reluctantly. The last batch she had skipped this entirely. She had kneaded maybe four minutes, decided her arms were tired, and let the dough rest its way into a loaf that crumbled when she cut it, weak where the network should have been strong. She could admit that now. What she could not decide was whether four minutes of honest tiredness was better or worse than eight minutes of performance, and she kept thinking about Mr. Hu, her old chemistry teacher, who used to say that a result you didn't like was still data. She had hated that sentence at fifteen. At sixteen, with flour on her forearms, she found it almost comforting.

She shaped the dough into a round, covered it with a damp towel, and put it near the window where the afternoon sun warmed the sill. While it rose she washed the counter and thought about the first loaf again, how she had wanted it to appear perfect and whole, metamorphic, as if it could change from ingredients into bread without her watching. That had been the real failure, she suspected. Not the kneading, though the kneading was part of it. The wanting to skip the middle part, where everything is sticky and shapeless and you have to keep folding it over itself.

Her mother came home at six with grocery bags and paused at the smell of yeast and warm flour. "Again?" she said, and Morgan could hear the question under the question, which was whether the first loaf had been a complaint about the store bread, about the household, about her.

"Again," Morgan said.

The second loaf came out of the oven at seven, darker than the first, singing faintly as its crust contracted in the air. They waited, because waiting was suddenly a thing Morgan believed in, and then she cut a slice. It tore a little at the edge of the knife, chewy, holding together, a network of holes inside where the gas had risen through it. She handed the slice to her mother across the counter, still steaming, and stood there with the knife in her hand while her mother took a bite.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: During Chuseok, Korea's harvest festival on the 15th day of the eighth lunar month, many families hold charye, a memorial rite that sets out food for their ancestors.
story:
My grandmother has this idea that I'm organized, which tells you how little she knows me, since the inside of my backpack is an archaeological site. But she announced in August that this year I would set the charye table myself, start to finish, because she was done doing it alone and my mother was done doing it wrong. Wrong, in my grandmother's vocabulary, is a technical term meaning "without me."

The dinner where this was decided was scathing on my mother's part and serene on my grandmother's, which is how their arguments always go, a blizzard against a stone wall. My mother thought it was too much pressure. My grandmother thought pressure was how you find out who a person is. I ate my rice and tried to become furniture.

So on the morning itself, the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month by the old calendar, which my grandmother recited like a password, I stood in her kitchen holding a plate of fried tofu and having no idea where it went. "It's charye," Ayden had said when I texted him a photo of the empty table the week before, because Ayden actually listens in world history. "The memorial rite. You set out food for the ancestors. It's part of Chuseok." I had replied with something dismissive about his being a know-it-all, and then I googled it for an hour, which is my usual process: insult, then secret research.

The table had rules, and the rules had reasons, and the reasons lived inside my grandmother's hands rather than in any list. Rice on the west, soup on the east, or was it the reverse. Fruit where the colors could be arranged by row. The tofu could go near the fish, I decided, or near the greens, and I moved it three times while my aunt watched from the doorway with the expression of a woman observing a tightrope walker who has not yet fallen but certainly will.

"What happens if I get it wrong?" I asked.

My grandmother was folding paper at the counter, not looking up. "The ancestors eat what you meant."

I want to be clear that this was not comforting. It was also, I suspected, not entirely an answer. Over the years I have learned that my grandmother's statements about the ancestors function less as theology than as a kind of oligarchy of the dead, a small unelected council whose opinions she happens to be the sole interpreter of, and whose rulings are suspiciously identical to her own. Thierry, when I described this theory to him, said, "That's every religion ever," and then, "also every group chat." Thierry is going to study anthropology or possibly nothing.

But here is the part I didn't expect. As I placed the chestnuts and the persimmons, as I set the rice bowls with their lids facing the way she indicated with one lifted finger, the table began to transfigure in front of me, the way a stage does between the last rehearsal and opening night. It stopped being an exam I was failing and became a message we were sending somewhere, addressed to people I had never met: her mother, her father, a brother who died young. She told me about the brother while I worked, unprompted, in the voice she uses for things that still hurt a little. He liked the fried tofu. That was why I was holding it.

I still put it on the wrong side, apparently, because she crossed the kitchen and slid the plate forty centimeters left without comment, and I laughed, and she allowed herself one small shrug that meant, in her language, close enough. Later, when the whole family stood and bowed toward the table, I bowed with everyone else and thought about the difference between doing something correctly and doing it at all, and how maybe my mother was right that it was too much pressure and my grandmother was right that pressure is the point, and how both of those could sit at the same table. When we raised our heads, my grandmother was looking at me instead of at the food.

"You'll do it again next year," she said.

I said, "I get a next year?" and she was already walking toward the kitchen to bring out the fruit she'd been hiding from my cousins.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: In C major the dominant seventh chord is G7, made of the notes G, B, D and F, and it pulls strongly toward the C major chord.
story:
Keira had agreed to write sixteen bars mostly to prove she could, and now the empty staff paper sat on the kitchen table radiating a kind of belligerent blankness, as if it dared her to make the fifth bar interesting. She had a melody, sort of. It wandered up from C, touched E, came home by way of G, and by bar fourteen it sounded like a song politely clearing its throat and then deciding not to sing. Her mom slid a mug of tea past the manuscript and said, "That's nice, honey," in the tone of a woman who could hear that it wasn't.

She texted Maverick a voice memo of the ending. He replied forty minutes later, from somewhere with wind in it: "it just stops. it's like when you wave at someone and they don't see you." Helpful. She texted Ophelia next, who was the sort of person who alphabetized her flashcards for fun. Ophelia's reply came in a burst of three messages: "okay so in C major you can make a chord on G", then "G B D and add F", then "it's called the dominant seventh, G7, and it pulls really hard toward the C chord. my mom calls it the drama chord." Keira read it twice, wrote G, B, D, F in the margin, and felt the specific exhilaration of being handed a key without being told which door it opened.

The problem was where. She tried the F in bar two, where it crashed against the E like two people reaching for the same door handle. She tried it in bar nine and it sulked. At the piano she played G, B, D alone, then G, B, D, F, back and forth, the way you'd tap two tiles to figure out which one was loose. The three-note version was pleasant, a handshake. The four-note version leaned. It sounded like a sentence that refused to end in a period.

Mr. Leung from next door chose that moment to water his window boxes, which meant he was audible through the screen. "You've played that bit eleven times," he called. "It's good. The wobbly one, with the extra note. Keep the wobbly one."

"It's not wobbly," Keira called back. "It's tense on purpose."

"Same thing," said Mr. Leung, and went inside.

She worked until the light went amber. Rather than guess at every bar, she decided to parametrize the whole thing: sixteen slots, a chord for each, the melody threaded through whatever the chord allowed. It made the composing feel less like inspiration and more like fitting groceries into a bag, which, honestly, she preferred. Bars one through eight fell into place. Bars nine through thirteen behaved. Bar fourteen kept its problem like a splinter.

Here is what she remembered, later, clearly: at some point past ten she had added the F to the chord in bar fifteen, played through, and the ending snapped into focus so hard she laughed out loud alone in the kitchen. Then she found a note on her phone she did not remember leaving herself: "the F before the last bar, that one, from Ophelia's thing." The handwriting was hers. The memory was not. She scrolled back through the texts, looking for the moment someone had told her to put it in the last approach bar, and found nothing. Ophelia had sent the chord; nobody had sent the placement.

She called Maverick, who answered mid-yawn. "I fixed my song," she said. "Ophelia gave me this chord, G7, it's G and B and D and then you add the F, and it pulls toward the C chord like a dog on a leash. I put it in bar fifteen so the last bar could just be C, and it works. It actually sounds finished."

"Congrats," said Maverick. "Who told you where to put it?"

"That's the thing," Keira said. She looked at the staff paper, at her own penciled F, at the dark window. "Nobody. I thought maybe you texted me something while I was half asleep, but I checked, and there's nothing. I guess I told myself and then forgot I was listening."

"Creepy," said Maverick happily. "Play it."

She put the phone on the piano lid, set her thumb on G, her fingers already reaching for B and D and the F waiting above them, and played bar fifteen into bar sixteen as Mr. Leung's kitchen light across the yard blinked off.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: To compare leases fairly, add the rent to every recurring cost the tenant pays, such as heat, electricity, water, internet and insurance, to get a total monthly cost.
story:
Jack had his driving lesson at six, which meant forty minutes in the lobby of Eze Defensive Driving with nothing to do but watch the crepuscular light fade over the parking lot and pretend the laminated posters about stopping distances were interesting. He spread the two leases across the plastic chairs instead, weighting their corners with his keys and a can of soda. One was for a third-floor unit on Marsh Street, seven hundred a month, heat included. The other was a basement on Culver, five ninety-five, nothing included. Jolene had sent him both photos that afternoon with the message "obviously Culver, look at the price," and Kristen had replied with a single skeptical question mark.

"Doing your homework in my lobby now," Mr. Eze said, coming out of the office with a clipboard. He was a large, unhurried man who had been desensitized, as far as Jack could tell, to every bad driver in the county; nothing students did behind the wheel surprised him anymore, and he said so with a kind of weary pride.

"Sort of," Jack said. "Apartment thing. Me and two friends are choosing a place for next year." He gestured at the pages. "This one's cheaper rent but the lease says tenant pays all utilities. The other one's more rent but heat's included."

Mr. Eze set the clipboard down and looked at the papers without touching them, the way he looked at a student's parallel parking, reserving judgment. "So what's the cheaper place?"

"That's the problem," Jack said. "I don't actually know yet."

He started listing on the back of a permission slip. Culver at five ninety-five, plus electricity, plus water, plus internet, plus insurance, plus heat, because the furnace was a separate meter and the tenant paid it, which he had only noticed on the third read. He called the utility office from the lobby's ancient wall phone and asked for last winter's averages for the address, and the woman on the other end gave him numbers in a bored, milky voice, as though reciting them had worn grooves in her. By the time he added it all, Culver came to something over eight hundred a month. Marsh Street, with its seven hundred and its included heat, plus electricity and internet and the rest, came to less.

The lobby's fluorescent hum filled the pause while he stared at his arithmetic. He checked it twice. The cheap rent was not the cheap place.

"Interesting," Mr. Eze said, and there was something in his voice that Jack filed away for later. "You want the total, not the headline. Every recurring cost, all in, then you compare."

"Yeah," Jack said slowly. "I mean, that's what the numbers say."

Jolene texted back within a minute of him sending the totals: "wait WHAT." Kristen wrote, "told you the question mark." For a while the three of them argued in short bursts, Jolene defending the basement's charm and its proximity to a diner, Kristen pointing out that a hundred dollars a month was a hundred dollars a month, and Jack sitting in the middle of it, aware that he had become the one with the spreadsheet, which was not a role he had ever held among them.
