It was nearly his lesson time when Mr. Eze, gathering the clipboard, said, "Marsh Street. The yellow building." Jack nodded. "My wife manages it," Mr. Eze went on, mild as anything. "I recognized the lease. The boiler's three years old and she replaces filters herself." He paused at the office door. "You'd have found that out anyway. You seem like the type who checks."

Jack laughed, a little thrown, a little reassured. He texted Jolene and Kristen one more line: "also the driving instructor's wife runs the yellow building, so, grain of salt, but the math still works." He gathered the leases, folded them into his jacket, and followed Mr. Eze out to the car, where the headlights swept the empty lot and the engine turned over on the first try.

"Mirrors first," Mr. Eze said, settling into the passenger seat. Jack adjusted the mirror and saw, reflected small in its corner, the two folded pages on the back seat, already half in shadow.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Cindy Sherman's Untitled Film Stills (1977 to 1980) is a series of 70 black-and-white photographs of herself posed as characters from imaginary movies.
story:
The summer before his application was due, Cole's mother drove him to his grandfather's house and left him there with two cameras, a box of film, and instructions to finish something. The assignment, given by Mr. Baptiste in the last week of school, was to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme, with an artist's statement, and Cole had spent June avoiding it. The theme he had chosen, half by accident, was self-portrait. He had said it out loud in class before he understood what it committed him to, and Eshal had laughed and said, "Ten pictures of your own face? Good luck making them different."

His grandfather was taciturn by noon and worse by evening, but in the mornings he made eggs and talked about the photographs he had taken in the sixties, of steel mills and men leaving shift, and he did not ask what Cole was doing at the kitchen table with the negatives spread out. On the third day he did ask, one word, "Stuck?" and Cole admitted it. He had taken four self-portraits by then, and they were all the same picture: Cole against the garage door, Cole against the fence, Cole by the porch rail, a boy looking slightly to the left of the lens with the same closed expression in every frame. "I picked a theme and now the theme is a cage," Cole said. His grandfather slid the eggs onto a plate and said, "Then pick a better door."

That afternoon Eshal biked over, having heard from Lorelei where he was hiding, and brought her along because she was the only person either of them knew who had actually read the whole art book from the library. She sat on the porch steps with the heavy book open on her knees while Cole explained his problem: how to make ten pictures of one subject that weren't ten copies of one picture. "Look," she said, and turned the book toward him. "Cindy Sherman. Untitled Film Stills, 1977 to 1980. It's seventy photographs, black and white, and she's in all of them, but she's posing as characters from movies that don't exist." Cole took the book and went through the pages slowly. A woman in a maid's uniform looking back over her shoulder. A woman in a trench coat on a windy street. A woman at a mirror, frightened of something outside the frame. Same face, seventy times, and not one of them the same person.

He was quiet long enough that Eshal said, "You've got that face you get when you're stealing something." Cole didn't argue. He went inside, found his grandfather's old hat rack and the trunk of clothes in the attic, and started pulling things out: a mechanic's coverall, a white dress shirt, a scarf that smelled of cedar and, faintly, of pipe smoke. "I'm not going to take pictures of me," he said, carrying the armload down the stairs. "I'm going to take pictures of people who don't exist, and all of them are going to be me." Lorelei said that sounded like a riddle, and Cole said he thought it was the whole point, though privately he wasn't sure it wasn't a trick he was playing on himself.

For four days he worked. He borrowed his grandfather's workshop lamp and hung a sheet for a backdrop. He shot himself as a night watchman, as a preacher, as a boy waiting outside a principal's office, as a man reading a letter with bad news on his face. His grandfather watched from the doorway the second evening, arms crossed, and finally said, "The one in the coveralls. That's your Uncle Ray. How'd you get him in there when he's been dead thirty years?" Cole said he didn't know, and it was the closest thing to praise he got all week.

The twist came when he printed the eighth photograph and showed the set to Eshal and Lorelei under the porch light. Lorelei went through them twice, then stopped at the earliest one, the boy against the garage door from before, the one Cole had almost thrown out. "Put this one in," she said. "Last. Or first." Eshal said that didn't make sense, it was the picture that had failed. Lorelei said that was why it worked, and the three of them argued about it until the porch light attracted moths and the argument dissolved into watching them.

Cole was still unsure. He had come to the house thinking a theme meant narrowing, choosing one thing and rejecting everything else, and now he was holding a portfolio that was one face pretending to be many people, ending with the picture where the pretending stopped. Or started. He couldn't decide which, and he said so, and Lorelei said, "Then say that in the statement. Say you don't know." Eshal, who had once refused to admit on a test that he'd guessed, looked at her as if she'd suggested showing up to an exam without a pencil. But she was already turning to Cole, pen out, and asked, "So what's the statement say? Give me the elocution." She grinned at the word, overformal on purpose.

"Something like," Cole said, and stopped, and started again. "Every one of these is me, and none of them are."

His grandfather came out with three glasses of iced tea and stood behind them, looking at the prints laid across the porch boards. He picked up the one of the boy against the garage door, held it to the light for a long moment, and set it back down at the front of the row.

"Keep that one first," he said, and went inside.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Many US colleges fill waitlist spots in May, after admitted students have sent deposits and the college knows how many places are still open.
story:
Morgan had told everyone that being waitlisted meant she was basically in, that it was a polite delay before the real acceptance, and she said it with such confidence that even her aunt had started calling it "the good news." She was sitting across from Ms. Chea in the guidance office, a folder of paperwork open between them, still saying it.

"So I wait," Morgan said. "That's the smart move. Why would I commit somewhere I don't want to be?"

Ms. Chea turned the folder so Morgan could see the deadline printed at the top of the other college's acceptance letter. May 1. The deposit was three hundred dollars.

"I can't pay three hundred dollars for a school I'm not going to," Morgan said.

"That's one way to look at it." Ms. Chea capped her pen and set it down. "Why don't you find out what actually happens to waitlists before you decide anything. Talk to someone who's been through it."

Morgan took this as agreement, more or less, and left the office feeling like she'd won something. She found Khalid at his locker and explained her situation, and he listened all the way through, which was unlike him.

"My brother got waitlisted two years ago," Khalid said. "He was number, like, nobody knows what number. But he told me the college didn't decide until May, because they wait for everyone's deposits to come in first. That's how they know how many spots are actually open." He shrugged. "So it was May, and by then he'd already put a deposit on his second choice. Nonrefundable."

Morgan said that sounded like bad luck, specific to his brother, and Khalid said maybe. But that night she looked it up herself, at the kitchen table with her mother watching television behind her, and the forums and the college's own admissions page said the same thing Khalid had. Waitlist spots fill in May, after admitted students send deposits and the college knows how many places are still open. Which meant the letter in her folder was not a delay of the answer. It was a structure, and it had a shape, and the shape put her decision at May 1, at three hundred dollars, before anyone would tell her anything.

She had also told everyone, at various points in the spring, that money wasn't really a factor, that her parents had it handled, and this was not exactly a lie so much as a hope she'd been speaking aloud. When she brought the deposit question to her mother, her mother said three hundred dollars was three hundred dollars, and asked whether the waitlisted school was giving financial aid if it came through. Morgan said probably. She did not know. She had applied early and never read the aid pages carefully, because she had assumed the whole thing would resolve itself, the way things in her life generally had.

She was debilitated by the choice for most of a week, which surprised her, since she'd always considered herself decisive. She lay on her bed with her laptop open on her stomach and read the admitted students page of her top choice over and over as though a new paragraph might appear. Ayanna came over on Thursday and sat on the floor painting her toenails, and Morgan laid the whole thing out for her, the May timeline, the nonrefundable deposit, the second school she actually liked fine but not in the way she liked the first one.

"Okay, but here's what I don't get," Ayanna said, blowing on her toes. "You keep calling the second school your backup like it's a punishment. You visited it. You said the campus was beautiful and the food was insane."

"That's not the point."

"It's a little the point. You described the dining hall to me for ten minutes. Ten minutes about a salad bar. That's the most hedonistic thing I've ever heard you say about anything."

Morgan laughed despite herself, and after Ayanna left she sat with it. There were two ways of thinking and she had been holding them like opposing teams. One said you commit fully to the thing you want and accept the risk, that half-measures debilitate the will and you get what you push for. The other said you build a life out of what's actually in front of you, and the campus with the salad bar and the good program and the friend who lived forty minutes away was not a consolation prize, it was a real place where real things would happen to her. On Friday she went back to Ms. Chea's office during her free period and put the folder on the desk.

"I'm paying the deposit," Morgan said. "The other school. And I'm staying on the waitlist anyway. If they take me in May, I decide then, and the three hundred dollars is just the price of getting to decide twice." She paused. "It's not indecision. I know that's what it looks like."

"It looks like a plan," Ms. Chea said, and slid the check form across the desk.

Morgan filled it out, and her hand was steady, and the pen caught on the paper at the dollar amount so she had to go over the zero twice. On the way out she passed the trophy case, and in the glass, faint over the tennis trophies, she could see her own reflection still standing in the doorway of the office, not moving yet, holding the receipt.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a vapor that irritates the eyes and makes them tear.
story:
The kitchen at Grandpa's house still smelled of the coffee he'd made at six in the morning, bitter and thick, and Alex liked arriving after it had cooled so the smell had soaked into everything, the curtains, the dish towels, the wooden spoon he was now holding like a question. He had promised to make the soup this time, the one with the chicken and the lemon and the rice that his grandmother used to make before her wrists gave out, and he had promised himself he would not call his mother for help even once. Lyvia was already at the counter with three onions and Mikhail was leaning against the fridge, arms folded, waiting to be entertained.

"You're going to cry," Mikhail said, not as a guess but as a forecast, the way he predicted everything, with total confidence and no evidence.

"Nobody's going to cry," Alex said, and Lyvia rolled her eyes at both of them and began peeling.

The recipe was not really a recipe. It lived in a stained notebook with a cracked spine, and Grandpa had set it on the counter without ceremony, the way he handed over anything that mattered to him, as though it were nothing. Their grandmother's handwriting sloped and faded in the later pages, and Alex had begun to wonder, paging through it, whether a thing like this could count as patrimony, an inheritance you could actually taste, or whether that word only applied to money and land and other dead things. He decided he'd ask no one and just believe it. He set the notebook open to the soup page and weighted it with the salt cellar.

Lyvia chopped the first onion and lasted about forty seconds. Then her eyes went glassy, then red, then streaming, and she laughed and swore and kept chopping anyway, wiping her face with her sleeve.

"You're crying over an onion," Mikhail said, delighted. "It's a vegetable, Lyvia."

"I'm not crying, it's, ugh, it's the onion, obviously it's the onion."

Mikhail's grin calcified into that particular smirk he wore when he thought he'd won something, and Alex felt the old pull to end it, to make some joke that would move the spotlight along. Instead he found himself actually wondering why the onion did that, because it was strange, wasn't it, that a plant would make you cry, that a vegetable could reach into your eyes from the cutting board. He rinsed his hands and picked up the notebook, but the soup page said nothing about tears. It just said, in his grandmother's hand, "onions, three, cut small."

The answer was in the back, where Grandpa kept newspaper clippings, and Alex nearly missed it. An old column about kitchen science, folded into quarters, and there it was in the second paragraph. He read it twice because the words were strange.

"Listen," he said. "Cutting an onion breaks its cells, and that releases enzymes that produce syn-propanethial-S-oxide."

"Say what?" Mikhail said.

"Syn-propanethial-S-oxide. It's a vapor. It irritates your eyes and makes them tear." He set the clipping on the counter between the onion skins and the lemon. "So she's not crying. Her eyes are getting attacked by a chemical weapon the onion makes when you cut it. She's basically under fire."

Lyvia, still streaming, pointed the knife at Mikhail. "Under fire," she said. "Tell him."

"Okay, but you still cried," Mikhail said, though less certainly now, and Alex thought about letting that go, too, because it was true in a way. The tears were real tears even if they weren't sad ones, and maybe it didn't matter much which kind you had, but that felt like a bigger idea than the kitchen could hold at eleven in the morning, so he held it quietly instead and decided he wasn't sure yet, and that not being sure felt less like losing than it used to.

Grandpa came in on his cane, looked at the counter, at the clipping, at Lyvia's wrecked face, and said, "That soup takes an hour. Start the chicken." Then he stood in the doorway a long moment, watching, and Alex chopped the next onion himself with his eyes stinging, and did not wipe them, and slid the pieces into the pot where the oil was just beginning to sing.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: According to the CDC, US drivers aged 16 to 19 have a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged 20 and older, per mile driven.
story:
Antoine had been waiting for this since the licensing office in March, when he stood in line behind a girl his age who kept rereading a poster on the wall while she waited for her permit test. She had turned around and said it to nobody in particular, the way people do when a fact has gotten under their skin. According to the CDC, drivers aged sixteen to nineteen in the United States had a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged twenty and older, per mile driven. She said it twice, as if repetition might soften it. Antoine had memorized it without meaning to, and now, six months later, the sentence sat in the passenger seat of Mr. Lawson's sedan like a third person.

"Mirror, signal, shoulder," Mr. Lawson said from beside him. He was a retired math teacher from the high school, and he taught driving the way he had taught geometry, with a patient faith that procedures, honestly followed, would carry you through. "Take it out to the end of the driveway and stop at the sidewalk."

Antoine turned the key. The car lurched, died, lurched again. On the third try it moved, and the whole machine reorganized itself around him, heavy and obedient and strange, like an animal deciding to trust him. He stopped where the driveway met the sidewalk, exactly, and felt a small pride that he immediately distrusted.

"Good. Left onto Marion, and keep it under twenty."

Marion Street was empty in the way of weekday mornings, its parked cars gleaming, its maples dropping the first brown leaves onto asphalt that had been poured over old alluvial ground, flat and soft-bottomed, the whole subdivision built where a river used to wander. Antoine steered and the car drifted toward the curb, corrected, drifted again. He was thinking about the poster girl, and about the number three, and about how the road did not care that he had passed his permit test on the first attempt.

Two blocks along, a girl stood at the bus shelter with her thumb in a book. Celia, from his statistics class. She looked up, saw the car, saw him, and her face did something complicated, surprise folding into amusement. She raised her hand, not exactly waving, more like flagging, and Antoine's foot went to the brake before he had decided anything.

"School's the other direction," Mr. Lawson observed.

"She's going to the community center. She told me yesterday, she volunteers Tuesdays." He eased the car forward again, slow. "Her bus doesn't come for another twenty minutes."

"Then the question is whether you're ready to have a passenger."

That was the question, and Antoine knew it was fair. He had believed, in a vague and comfortable way, that passing tests translated into deserving things, that the whole system was a meritocracy and the permit was his first certificate in it. But the girl at the licensing office had been standing in line to pass her own test, and the poster had still been speaking to her. The statistic didn't care what he'd earned. It took his age and reified it, turned him into one instance of a category, and the category died at nearly three times the rate of everyone older, per mile. He could resent that or he could take it seriously, and those were not the same as disagreeing with it.

"Pull over at the shelter," Mr. Lawson said, "and let's think."

Antoine pulled over, hands at ten and two, and rolled down the passenger window. Celia leaned in, book against her collarbone. "You're driving," she said. "Like a real person."

"It's my first lesson," he said. "That's the whole situation. First one."

"So don't offer me a ride."

"I wasn't going to." He hesitated, because that wasn't quite true; his hand had already imagined opening the door. "The CDC says drivers my age have a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers twenty and older, per mile. Almost exactly three. I keep thinking about it and I can't decide if it's a reason or just a number."

Celia considered him for a moment. "It's both," she said. "Take the bus with me, if you're worried. We can be statistically boring together."

"Wednesday," he said. "Wednesday I'll know how to drive a little."

"Then Wednesday you can be boring at me." She stepped back from the window and tapped the roof of the car twice, a small percussive kindness, and returned to her bench with her book.

Antoine checked the mirror, signalled, and pulled out onto Marion Street, his line of travel only slightly crooked, the leaves breaking softly under the tires.

"Better," Mr. Lawson said. "Now, without the word almost, how far do you trust that number?"

"Farther than I trust myself," Antoine said, and slowed for the stop sign at Fenwick, pressing the pedal down gradually, both hands steady on the wheel.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: The Situation-Behavior-Impact model, from the Center for Creative Leadership, frames feedback by naming when it happened, what the person did, and what effect it had.
story:
The kitchen smelled like burnt basil, which did not presage anything good about the group project, only about Greta's mother's attempts at dinner. Camille sat at the counter with her laptop open to the shared document, cursor blinking after the words Marcus still hasn't turned in the methodology section. She deleted them, retyped them, deleted them again.

"You're hovering," Greta said, sliding a glass of water across the marble. "Just tell him he's lazy and get it over with."

Camille didn't want to tell Marcus he was lazy. She wanted him to actually finish the section, and she suspected, though she couldn't prove it, that calling him lazy would accomplish the opposite. She said so, and Greta rolled her eyes with the fond exasperation of someone who had heard Camille reason her way through small moral problems before.

Then Greta's mother came through trailing the smell of the oven, dropped a binder on the counter beside the fruit bowl, and went back out again, calling something about the smoke alarm. Camille, grateful for the interruption, flipped it open out of idle curiosity. It was a training manual from her work, something about leadership. One page had been flagged with a pink sticky note. The heading read Situation-Behavior-Impact.

Greta leaned over her shoulder. "Oh, that. She goes on about it constantly. It's from the Center for Creative Leadership or somewhere like that. You name the situation, then the behavior, what the person actually did, then the impact it had." She plucked a grape from the bowl. "Basically it stops you being an apologist for people, or a monster to them."

Camille read the page twice. It was almost embarrassingly simple, and yet it had rearranged something in her head, the way a diagram rearranges a sentence you thought you understood. You're lazy was a verdict, handed down from nowhere, about everything. But Friday's deadline, the methodology section wasn't turned in, and now we're two days behind on the analysis. That was a thing that had happened, and a thing a person could respond to. What stayed uncertain, she thought, closing the binder, was whether Marcus would hear even that kindly, or whether he'd decided she was the enemy weeks ago and nothing she said would land.

She drafted the message on her phone while Greta washed dishes with more force than the dishes required.

"Hey. Can we talk about Friday? The methodology section was due then and it didn't come in, and now we can't start the analysis, so the whole timeline is tight. I know the section is the worst part of this project. What's going on with it, and can I help?"

She read it aloud. Greta said it sounded like a hostage negotiation, but a nice one, and pressed send before Camille could second-guess the word tight.

His reply came as she was pulling on her jacket to leave. She expected an excuse, or the recalcitrant silence he'd perfected in the group chat, the kind that made even the teachers stop asking. Instead there were three messages, then a photograph. The first message said, Fair. The second said, Can I show you something first, before you decide I'm useless. The third was a screenshot, and the photograph was of his notebook, dense with hand-drawn tables, margins full of arrows, a methodology section so overbuilt it had sprouted appendices no one had asked for. He hadn't been lazy. He had been drowning in exactly the part he'd promised to do.

Camille stood in Greta's hallway with her boots half on, staring at it. She had spent four days composing an accusation in her head, sharpening it, softening it, and the whole time the real problem had been sitting in a notebook three streets away, too large to submit and too far along to abandon.

She typed back, "Come to Greta's tomorrow. Bring the notebook. We'll cut it down together, and I'll take the appendices." Then she added, because it seemed only honest, "Also you don't get to just go silent on us. That part still happened."

Greta appeared at the end of the hall, towel over her shoulder, and mouthed, Well? Camille turned the phone around so she could see the photograph of the notebook, tables blooming outward like frost on glass.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas, but it acts mainly as a feedback: warmer air holds more water vapor, which amplifies warming started by other gases like carbon dioxide.
story:
The science museum had given the debate team its education room for the afternoon, a glass-walled box beside the climate exhibit, and Camille had claimed the seat closest to the graph. It ran the length of one wall, carbon dioxide over the past century, a line that climbed in small stuttering steps, dipped twice, and then rose as though it had lost patience with its own history. She had seen versions of it before, in textbooks and on screens, but the scale of this one made her feel she was standing inside the numbers.

"You're staring again," Simon said, dropping into the chair beside her. He spread his cue cards across the table like a dealer in a game she hadn't agreed to play.

"I'm reading."

"You're glowering. There's a difference." He tapped the graph's final rise, the steep part, the part everyone quoted. "This is all you need. Up, up, up. The rest is decoration."

Beckett arrived late, coat still on, holding the folder with their assigned positions. The regional tournament was in eleven days, and the motion concerned carbon regulation. He read the pairings, and Camille's name came up against his for the practice round, which was how she ended up arguing the side she privately distrusted, the side that said the science was less settled than it looked.

She built her case carefully, almost regretfully, and it was going well until the scrimmage's third minute, when Simon, playing cross-examination, leaned into the microphone with the expression of someone about to enjoy himself. "Isn't it true," he said, "that water vapor, not carbon dioxide, is the real driver of the greenhouse effect? Isn't your whole case built on the wrong molecule?"

The room went quiet in the way rooms do when a question lands harder than its asker intended. Camille looked at the graph. She had read the museum's plaques twice that morning, and one of them surfaced now, not as an answer but as an irritation at the edge of her memory, something about abundance and something about order.

"Water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas," she said slowly. "That part's true." Simon smiled, and she watched the smile, and understood that the smile was the trap, that the fact he'd handed her was a door that only opened one way if you pushed it in ignorance. "But it acts mainly as a feedback," she went on. "Warmer air holds more water vapor, and that amplifies warming that got started by other gases. Like carbon dioxide. So it's not the cause. It's the echo that gets louder."

Beckett let out a breath. Simon sat back, riffling his cards, and Ms. Chaudhry, who had been leaning against the glass wall taking notes, wrote something without looking up. Camille felt the strange flatness of having turned a question, the sensation less like victory than like catching a glass before it hit the floor: nobody applauds, and your wrist aches.

"Where'd you get that?" Simon asked, genuinely curious, the performance dropped.

"The plaques. By the cloud chamber. I read them while you were buying chips."

"That's cheating."

"That's Saturday."

The practice round collapsed into argument after that, the good kind, the kind where Beckett kept saying "but then the ocean," and Simon kept saying "but then the economy," and nobody won because the motion was not a thing that could be won, only carried. Camille found herself doing the arithmetic Ms. Chaudhry had set them for homework, the exercise about which policy would sequester the most carbon by 2050, and noticing that every answer cost something: the forest plan ate farmland, the capture plan ate money nobody had voted for, the doing-nothing plan ate the graph. She had wanted, all season, for debate to feel like mathematics, where being right was verifiable, and instead it kept feeling like translation, from a science whose vernacular she was only beginning to speak into a language of voters and budgets where words stretched.

Afterward the team packed up and drifted toward the exit and the rain, and Camille stayed behind at the wall. Ms. Chaudhry was stacking chairs, and Camille asked her, quietly, whether the feedback point would hold up in the actual round, whether the judges would let it stand or whether someone would twist it further than Simon had.

"Twist it how?" Ms. Chaudhry asked.

"I don't know yet. That's the problem."

Ms. Chaudhry considered the graph, and the rain on the glass, and did not offer reassurance, which Camille recognized as a kind of respect. "You'll find out when they do it," she said, and carried two chairs to the corner.

Simon came back for his forgotten cards and stood beside Camille at the wall. "You were petulant in the last exchange, by the way," he said. "When I cut you off. The judges will mark it."

"I wasn't petulant, I was right."

"Those aren't opposites." He picked up his cards, squared them, and looked at the line climbing the wall. Outside, the rain had thickened, and somewhere in the parking lot a horn sounded twice, impatient, calling someone home. Camille zipped her bag and pulled her hood up and followed him out into the water-heavy air.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: The CDC advises against washing raw chicken, because the splashing water can spread bacteria to the sink and nearby surfaces.
story:
The assignment on the board said "A Dish From Home," which meant the cooking classroom would smell like thirty different childhoods by three o'clock. Alexander had signed up to make his grandmother's arroz con pollo, mostly so he could stop describing it to people and start handing them a plate. He'd watched her make it a hundred times, and every time it began the same way: cold water running, the chicken held under it, her hands turning the pieces over like she was polishing stones.

He set the cutting board by the sink, opened the package of thighs, and turned the tap on. August, working at the next station on some triumphant lasagna, looked up with the expression of a person watching someone step into traffic.

"Don't," August said.

"It's just a rinse."

"Put the chicken down and step away from the sink."

Alexander did not put the chicken down. He held it over the running water and raised an eyebrow, which was the level of debate his family usually settled things at. August crossed the aisle, turned the tap off with one hand, and pointed at Alexander's chicken with the seriousness of a customs officer.

"The CDC advises against washing raw chicken," August said. "The splashing water spreads bacteria to the sink and the nearby surfaces."

"That's the weirdest sentence anyone has ever said to me in this building, and I once watched a kid argue with a vending machine."

"Look it up. It's real. There's a whole page about it."

Alexander looked at his chicken, which sat in his hands looking, he had to admit, exactly as unwashed as before. His grandmother had rinsed chicken in that sink since before he was born, and nobody in his family had ever grown a second head. On the other hand, August had once been right about the vending machine kid too, which was a low bar, but still. The class around them churned on: Cole across the room negotiating loudly with a recalcitrant dough that refused to roll flat, Ms. Wong drifting between stations like a judge at a small, floury Olympics.

He dried his hands and typed into his phone, keeping one eye on August in case this turned out to be an elaborate prank. It did not turn out to be an elaborate prank. There it was, plain as a bus schedule, the same fact in the same words, on a page that clearly had better things to do than lie to him about sinks.

"So what do I do," he said, "just, cook it? Cook it dirty?"

" Cooked is the word you want. Cooked through is what makes it safe. Rinsing doesn't do anything except redecorate the counter."

"My grandmother washed it every single time."

"And I bet her grandmother believed you had to scare eggs before beating them. Traditions don't have to be wrong to be old." August softened, because August could tell when a dish meant something. "Look, keep everything else the same. The sofrito, the saffron if you're fancy, which you're not. Nobody's taking your grandmother's recipe. Just skip one step."

Alexander stood there a moment with the tap silent behind him, weighing two ways of knowing. His grandmother's kitchen had its own physics, tested across decades of Sunday afternoons, and it had never once poisoned him. But this was the trouble with growing up, he supposed: you ended up standing in a school kitchen at seventeen, holding raw chicken, having to decide whether love and evidence were allowed to disagree. He suspected the honest answer was that they could, and that you got to choose anyway.

He salted the thighs and laid them skin-down in the pan, feeling faintly like a traitor and faintly like a scientist. The skin hissed. He built the sofrito slow, onion then pepper then garlic, and when the rice went in and the saffron bloomed orange across the surface, the station smelled exactly like her kitchen, which startled him. He'd expected the dish to be missing something, some invisible cleanliness, and instead it was all there. At the end of class he packed a container for his family and kept a spoonful for August, who tasted it and pronounced it better than the lasagna, though the lasagna had collapsed in the oven like a small archipelago and was in no condition to compete.

At home his younger brother leaned over the container, sniffing, suspicious of good news. "You washed the chicken, right?"

Alexander considered the question, the whole evening balanced on it, and handed him a fork.

"Eat," he said.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In soccer, being in an offside position is not an offence by itself; a player is penalized only when involved in active play, and there is no offside from a throw-in, goal kick or corner.
story:
The screen above the bar filled half the wall, and Aiden had the seat with the best view, which his uncle kept trying to take from him by scooting his chair sideways an inch at a time. It was the semifinal, and the whole extended family had colonized the long table by the window: his parents, his uncle, Morgane and Deanna from his econ class, and Mr. Mensah, their old neighbor, who ordered nothing but black coffee and picked at a basket of chips with the discipline of an ascetic refusing everything richer. In the fourteenth minute a corner kick swung in and a striker rose above everyone and headed it into the net, and his uncle was on his feet before the ball finished rattling the goal.

"Offside! He was three meters past the last defender, are you blind?" His uncle waved his arm at the screen as though the referee could feel the breeze.

"That's not offside," Aiden said, and immediately wished he had said it more quietly, because now everyone was looking at him.

"How do you figure, you're the expert now?"

Aiden had read the Laws of the Game twice the summer before, mostly out of boredom, partly because he liked knowing how a system of rules tried to see everything at once. "There's no offside from a corner," he said. "You can't be offside from a throw-in or a goal kick either." His uncle started to remonstrate, finger raised, but the referee on screen pointed to the center circle and the replay rolled, and the whole table watched the corner taker's foot strike the ball with no whistle anywhere in the sequence.

"So you can stand in an offside position and nothing happens?" Deanna said, tearing a piece of naan in half.

"You can stand wherever you want," Aiden said. "Being in an offside position isn't an offence by itself. You only get penalized if you're involved in active play. So if you're off past the last defender but the ball never comes near you, the referee just lets it go." He heard himself sounding like a textbook and dialed it back. "Basically the rule punishes what you do, not where you stand."

Morgane, who argued about everything and enjoyed it, set down her fork. "So the whole thing is about intention, kind of. Where you are doesn't matter until you act." She looked pleased with herself, and Aiden found himself wondering whether that was actually true, whether a rule could really be about intention at all, or whether it was just about a moment in time, the instant the ball was played, frozen and judged. He had never thought of the law as something that had to choose between those two ideas, and now that he saw the seam in it he could not stop looking.

"Either way, it's a goal," his uncle said, sitting back down, though he squeezed Aiden's shoulder on the way, which in his uncle's language was a full apology. "You knew that off the top of your head?"

"I looked it up once. I got a call wrong in a game I was reffing for the little kids' league and I felt bad about it." He had sent off a seven-year-old's goal that had come from her teammate's throw-in, and she had cried, and afterward the league coordinator had told him the throw-in part and Aiden had gone home and read everything, mostly, he thought now, to make it up to a girl whose name he never learned. There was something almost altruistic in trying to learn a rule perfectly for people you would never see again, or maybe it was just guilt wearing a nicer shirt.

The match went on. In the thirty-second minute a winger lingered in what Aiden could now see clearly was an offside position, arms wide, plainly baiting the pass, and when the ball came he touched it and the flag went up, and Aiden leaned forward because he wanted to watch the referee make the distinction in real time, the same rule breathing in two different ways within twenty minutes. Mr. Mensah caught his eye over the rim of his coffee cup.

"So," Mr. Mensah said, "tell me, was that one offside, or is my television about to be corrected again?"

"Offside," Aiden said. "He touched it. Active play."

"Then I'll trust the referee," Mr. Mensah said, and lifted his cup toward the screen as the winger walked back, shaking his head, still arguing.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own, published in 1929, argues that a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction.
story:
Ashton had claimed the table by the window on the second floor of the public library, where the afternoon light came through in long panels and the radiators ticked. He spread out his copy of Jane Eyre, his notebook, and the assignment sheet Ms. Carvalho had handed out two days before: apply a critical lens to one passage from the novel, any lens, but apply it honestly. He had chosen the passage where Rochester disguises himself as a gypsy and reads Jane's fortune, mostly because he could picture the scene, and partly because he had no idea what to say about it.

"Is this seat taken?" Imogen stood with her own stack of books, a sociology thing and two novels he didn't recognize. He shook his head and she sat down across from him, arranging her things with the care of someone settling in for hours. She was applying early decision to a program that wanted evidence of independent reading, and she had decided the library was where she would manufacture that evidence. She wanted, he knew, to fill a page of her application with the titles of books she had actually finished.

They worked in a quiet that lasted almost twenty minutes. Then she looked up at his assignment sheet. "What's a critical lens, actually?"

"A way of reading. Like asking who has the money in the story, and who doesn't." He turned the notebook toward her. He had written a question at the top of the page, the question he'd asked Ms. Carvalho after class on Tuesday: why were so few of the classic novels on the reading list written by women? He had been counting, out of a boredom that turned into something sharper, and the count had bothered him enough that he'd stayed behind. Ms. Carvalho hadn't answered with a lecture. She had gone to the shelf behind her desk, taken down a thin book, and set it in front of him. "Virginia Woolf," she'd said. "A Room of One's Own. Published in 1929. Read the first chapter and tell me what you think."

Imogen pulled the Woolf toward her and read with her chin propped on her fist. Ashton went back to his passage. Jane, he noticed, had five pounds a year, a governess's wages, and no room that was hers; every room in Thornfield belonged to Rochester, down to the gypsy costume he wore like another property. Woolf's argument, which he now understood she had laid out plainly on those first pages, was that a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction. He had first taken that literally, and then, looking at Jane's situation, less so. Maybe the same conditions underpinned a woman's speaking in a novel, not just her writing one. Jane could refuse the fortune-teller's flattery because she had wages, tiny as they were. Whether she could have refused Rochester himself was a different question, and one the book kept postponing.

"So this is about writers," Imogen said, tapping the Woolf. "Not characters."

"Maybe both. That's what I can't decide." He showed her his two columns, one headed Marxist, one headed feminist, and the notes spilling between them. Under Marxist he had written that Rochester's disguises were what wealth let him do, that hedonism of that kind, dressing up, traveling, buying and abandoning, was a rich man's sport, and that Jane's plainness of dress was an economy forced on her rather than chosen. Under feminist he had written that Jane was being read like a text by a man who already owned the room she sat in. The two lenses overlapped almost everywhere, and where they didn't, he wasn't sure which one to trust.

Imogen read his columns with real attention, which she did not always give his schoolwork. "You could just say they're the same thing."

"But they're not. Woolf says money and a room. Marx would say the room is the point and the money is who owns you. A woman could have wages and still have no room that anyone had to knock before entering." He heard his own voice rise slightly and lowered it, because the librarian had passed behind them with a cart of returns. "I think that's the difference. I think. I'm not sure the difference survives the whole novel."

"Then say that," Imogen said. "You're allowed to not be sure. My whole application is me pretending to be sure." She said it lightly, but she looked down at her list of titles after she said it, and he understood that the page of finished books had stopped growing weeks ago, and that she knew it.

Ashton wrote one more line at the bottom of the page, then closed the notebook and rested his hand on it. Imogen went back to her sociology book. Across the room, the librarian slid a return into its place on the shelf, and the light through the window had shifted so that it fell now on the Woolf rather than on the Jane Eyre.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: A digital elevation model is a raster layer storing the ground height of each cell, which GIS uses to predict where water will flow and collect.
story:
The travel agency stayed open until six, and after that Juliette had the place to herself, more or less, because Mr. Paquette let her use the back computer for her geography project as long as she stacked the brochures first. She had spent two evenings stacking pamphlets for cruises she would never take, and now the third evening was hers. The agency smelled of toner and the fake leather of the chairs where couples sat to plan honeymoons, and behind her the big paper map of the world hung with its continents slightly curled at the corners, an older genealogy of the place, drawn back when people still came in person to find out where a road went.

The problem was a street called Alver Road. On her flood risk map it showed orange, high risk, though it stood nearly a kilometre from the river, farther than her own house, which showed a placid blue. Her first thought was that the data was wrong, that some clerk had mistyped a number, and she had almost written that in her notes for Mr. Paquette's Tuesday session. But Kellen, when she showed him the map on her phone between classes, had only leaned closer and said, "Look at the shape of the orange. It follows a line, like a wrinkle."

"Streets don't wrinkle," Juliette said, but that evening, at the back computer, she did what she should have done first. Her map was built from layers, stacked like transparencies on an overhead projector, and each layer could be turned on or off. She had been staring at the flood layer and the housing layer together for so long that she had forgotten the layers underneath existed. She turned off the housing layer first, then the flood layer, and turned on the one marked elevation.

The screen went grey and green, low ground dark and high ground pale, and Alver Road lay in a long dark tongue that ran downhill from nowhere near the river toward a basin near the railway cut. She had assumed the river was the only water that mattered. The map disagreed.

Rose came by the agency at closing to walk home with her and stood over the keyboard with her coat still on. "What's that, a heat map of boredom?"

"It's the elevation," Juliette said. "It's called a digital elevation model. It's a raster layer, so it's all these little cells, and each cell stores the ground height."

Rose bent closer, until her breath fogged the screen's cold. "So it's the ground itself."

"It's what the computer uses to figure out where water will go," Juliette said. "Where it'll flow and where it'll collect." She traced the dark tongue with her finger, not touching the glass. "That's Alver Road. It's a low spot. Water runs into it from the higher streets around it, even though it's nowhere near the river."

Mr. Paquette locked the front door and came back to stand behind them, reading over their shoulders the way he read itineraries, silently, twice. "My uncle lived on a street like that," he said at last. "Every spring the water came up through the storm drain and he would stand in his kitchen in rubber boots, expostulating at the ceiling." He straightened the brochures she had stacked, though they were already straight. "He was two miles from any river. Everyone said he was imagining it, because everyone believes water only comes from the thing you can see."

Juliette sat back down. She added the housing layer again over the elevation, and then the flood layer, and the three of them agreed under the light of the one lamp that stayed on after hours. The houses on Alver Road were mostly rentals, small lots, older buildings, the kind of block where the flood risk had been orange for years without anything being done, and she understood now that the orange was not an error or a mystery but an argument the city had made without saying it out loud. Water collects in low places; low places are often cheap places; cheap places fill with people who did not choose the low ground so much as inherit it. She had wanted the map to be a clean answer, a fact that would sit still on the page, and instead it was this, one truth laid over another, each one partial.

She wrote Alver Road at the top of a fresh page and underneath it a question she could not yet answer: who had decided where the storm drains went, and when, and whether anyone had looked at this same grey and green screen and then looked away. Her father would say she was overcomplicating it, that water goes downhill and that's the whole story. He was not wrong. But the map held both things at once, the physics and the streets, and she was beginning to think that keeping both in view was the actual skill, the one nobody had put on the assignment sheet.

Rose tugged her sleeve. "It's dark out."

"Two minutes." Juliette exported the map, saved it twice, and then turned the monitor off. The world map on the wall behind her caught the streetlight through the front glass, its continents faded and curling, no elevations at all, just the shapes people had agreed to draw.

On the walk home Rose asked whether the project was about flooding or about houses, and Juliette said, honestly, that she didn't know yet, and kept walking.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: Economists count the wages a student gives up while studying full-time as part of the cost of college, along with tuition.
story:
Naomi had been holding the same matte envelope for six days, unopened, turning it over like a coin she was afraid to flip. She brought it to the coffee shop on Miller Street because her room had begun to feel like a courtroom, and she wanted witnesses she wasn't related to.

Gabriella claimed the booth by the window and slid a menu across as though it were a legal document. "You're opening it here. Non-negotiable. I beseech you." She flattened her hand on the table, palm up, waiting. Cailyn came back from the counter with three hot chocolates nobody had ordered and one straw she insisted was for sharing.

"Full scholarship to Dawson," Naomi said, before opening anything, which was cheating, and both of them knew it. "If I defer, I keep the job at the clinic. Full time, benefits, the whole package." She said it quickly, the way you say a thing you've already argued with yourself about for six nights.

"Defer for what?" Cailyn asked. "A job?"

"The job is nineteen dollars an hour."

Gabriella leaned back. "Okay, but tuition at Dawson is basically nothing for you now. That's free college."

"Nothing plus everything I'd not be earning," Naomi said, and then stopped, because she wasn't sure she'd said that right, and Ms. Siddiqui, who owned the shop and had come over to wipe their table with a cloth that had seen better decades, paused with the rag in midair.

"Say that again," Ms. Siddiqui said. Not unkindly. She had a way of standing that suggested she had heard every argument ever made in her booths and had adjudicated most of them.

"The wages," Naomi said slowly, hearing it take shape as she spoke. "While I'm studying full time, I can't work full time. Economists count that. The money I give up, the paycheck I could be earning instead, that's part of what college costs, on top of tuition. Not just the bill. The bill plus the job I'm not doing." Ms. Siddiqui nodded once, as if confirming a delivery, and moved on to the next table.

The shop hummed around them. The espresso machine made its laborious dying-swan noise; Ms. Siddiqui muttered that the thing was obsolescent and she would mourn it when it finally went. Gabriella was doing math on a napkin, multiplication marching crookedly down the paper. "Four years of nineteen an hour, full time," she said. "That's, like. A car. Several cars. A house, in some towns."

"And tuition at Dawson," Cailyn said, "for you, is a rounding error. So actually college costs way more than people think, even free college." She looked proud of herself, then doubtful. "Wait. That can't be right."

"It's right," Naomi said. "It's just not the whole question."

Cailyn sucked the shared straw with unnecessary force. "Then what is the whole question?"

"That's what the envelope is," Naomi said.

She opened it finally, and the slow part began. The flap resisted. Her thumbnail caught the paper the way a key catches in an old lock, and Gabriella held her breath so audibly that a man at the next table glanced over. Inside was a single sheet, and Naomi read it twice, and then a third time, because the first two readings she was only looking at the word DEFER in bold at the top and not at anything under it. The scholarship could be held for one year. One year, not more. If she took the clinic job for a year, she kept the scholarship; if she stayed at the clinic past that, Dawson closed the door and she would be applying all over again, at twenty, against everyone fresh out of high school, with a résumé that said she'd once chosen a paycheck.

"One year," she said out loud. "The deferral is one year."

Gabriella put down the napkin. "So the question isn't job versus college."

"It's job for one year versus the next four," Naomi said. "And whether the year buys me enough to make the other four harder." She was surprised to find she had already tipped in one direction, that some part of her had decided in the car, in the shower, in the six nights of courtroom darkness, and had only been waiting for the rest of her to catch up. A year of wages, saved, meant graduating without loans that her friends would be carrying. A year of clinic work meant four years of wondering whether the door would have opened twice. Both were true at once. She could hold them together without pretending one was casuistry and the other gospel, though it took effort, like carrying two full cups through a crowded room.

She turned the envelope over. On the back, in the pen of some anonymous admissions officer, someone had written "Reply by June 1," and underlined June 1 twice.

"I'll take the year," she said. "Then Dawson. That's the answer unless I hate the clinic, which I won't, because I already work Saturdays and I mostly love it, except for the filing, which is the eighth circle."

Cailyn raised the shared straw like a toast. Gabriella flagged Ms. Siddiqui down and ordered three of the most expensive things on the menu, which turned out to be the same hot chocolates they already had.

Naomi laughed until the napkin math smeared under her wrist. She slid the letter into her jacket, next to her heart, where it would ride home slightly bent.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: The 1987 Montreal Protocol, which phases out ozone-destroying chemicals, was the first treaty in United Nations history to be ratified by every UN member state.
story:
The city's public works annex smelled of wet cardboard and toner, and Audrey had learned, in her first week of the internship, which of its printers jammed and which door you had to lift slightly to close. Her job was supposed to be filing flood maps, but by Thursday of the second week she had been pulled into something larger: the stormwater fee proposal, a modest charge on impervious surfaces that would pay for the creek restoration everyone claimed to want and no one claimed to want to pay for. Her supervisor, a tired planner named only in emails as the stormwater coordinator, had a petition on her desk with four hundred signatures against it.

"It's not even the money for most of them," the coordinator said, squinting at a spreadsheet. "It's the principle. People think a fee on their driveway is the city reaching into their pockets." She slid the opposition list across the desk. "You know the neighborhood associations? Start there. Find out who's organizing."

Audrey did not expect Keon. She had known him since sophomore chemistry, where he'd been the one who argued, cheerfully and at length, that any tax was basically theft. Now he was standing at his grandmother's mailbox on Ashland Street with a flyer from the opposition, and when he saw her clipboard he laughed and held it up like a shield. "You're the enemy now. They sent a seventeen-year-old."

"I'm an intern," Audrey said. "I file things. Occasionally I'm allowed to knock on doors."

"Come in, then. Giovanni's here. We're making an argument out of it, actually. Whitehead assigned this debate for the fall, whether countries can ever agree on an environmental problem, and I'm taking the no side. Countries can't even agree on a driveway fee. Same species of problem, bigger scale." He waved her toward the porch. His grandmother brought out lemonade without being asked, a small authority that required no ratification.

Inside, Giovanni was sitting on the floor with a laptop, and he turned the screen around before Audrey had set down her glass. "The ozone treaty," he said. "Look. The 1987 Montreal Protocol, the one that phases out ozone-destroying chemicals. It was the first treaty in United Nations history to be ratified by every UN member state." He said it again, slower, as if testing the weight of each clause. "Every single one. That's the whole world agreeing."

"Agreeing to what, though," Keon said, and got up to look over his shoulder. "Paper agreement. Half of them probably signed it and did nothing."

From where Audrey sat she could see the flyer on the table, its bold type listing the neighborhoods that would pay the fee, and she thought about the four hundred signatures and the coordinator's spreadsheet, the way money moved through the city like water under a pavement no one wanted to lift. The creek flooded every third year now. The maps she filed showed it plainly, blue creeping over blocks that had been dry in older maps, an exhumed fact the city kept digging up and reburying. She said, "People around here can't agree on anything either. But the treaty happened."

"Fine," Keon said. "One counterexample."

"One counterexample," Giovanni said, "that happens to be the whole planet."

Keon was quiet for a while after they left the porch. He walked Audrey two blocks toward the annex, hands in his pockets, and when he finally spoke it was not to concede, exactly, but to move somewhere nearby. "Maybe the no side isn't that they can't agree," he said. "Maybe it's that they only agree when the thing they're fixing is far away and slow. Nobody's driveway is in Antarctica." He stopped at the corner. "I might switch sides, though. Argue the yes and make the no side say why the ozone layer was easier than a creek. That's harder to answer."

"That's not switching sides," Audrey said. "That's making the question better."

Back at the annex the next morning, the coordinator was on the phone, and when she hung up she looked, for once, not tired but almost pleased. The petition's organizer had called. It had turned out that the man circulating the flyers owned the paving company that resurfaced the church lot, and the church lot, according to the county assessor, was the largest impervious parcel in the watershed. The opposition had not been about principle after all, or not only. The coordinator slid the assessor's printout across the desk to Audrey, an antiquity of a document, the parcel lines drawn by hand in 1961.

"So what do I do with this?" Audrey asked.

"Nothing, yet," the coordinator said. "You file it. But sometimes, when you exhume why people are against something, you find the reason was never buried very deep." She turned back to her spreadsheets. Audrey took the printout to the records room, set it in its folder, and then took it out again to read the penciled note in the margin, a name she recognized from the flyer in Keon's hand.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Under the US Fair Labor Standards Act, non-exempt employees must be paid one and a half times their regular rate for hours worked beyond 40 in a workweek.
story:
Anais had been at Kessler's Grocery for eleven days when she agreed to cover Deli on Saturday, and then Bakery on Sunday, and then the registers for two evening shifts because the assistant manager said please, and because she wanted the money for textbooks, and because she had not yet learned that a week of work did not reset on Monday the way a school week did. She liked the job more than she had expected to. The produce cooler smelled like wet green things, and the older woman who ran the register, who had worked there since the store had a butcher counter, called her "sweetheart" without any of the condescension Anais usually bristled at.

Her friend Chase had been skeptical from the start. "Jobs like that ossify you," he had said over iced tea in July, meaning it half-seriously, the way he said most things. "You'll be there twenty years and one day you'll look up from the register and realize you can't remember deciding anything." Chase was applying to schools far away and spoke about her staying in town as though it were a surrender rather than a choice. Flora, who was staying too, had taken Anais's side, more or less. "Or she earns money and buys her own things," Flora had said. "Not everything is a referendum on your soul."

The Thursday before her second full week, Anais clocked out and checked her hours on the schedule taped by the time clock. She counted them twice, pressing each number with her finger. Forty-six. She had worked forty-six hours, most of them fine and a few of them good, the Saturday deli shift surprisingly satisfying, slicing turkey for a man who told her about his granddaughter's graduation. But something about the number felt off, and not only because it was more than she had meant to work.

At home she looked it up on her phone, sitting on her bedroom floor with the door open because her mother was watching TV in the next room. The page she found, plain and official, said that under the Fair Labor Standards Act, non-exempt employees must be paid one and a half times their regular rate for hours worked beyond 40 in a workweek. She read it three times. She was non-exempt; she had checked the box on her paperwork without understanding what the box meant. One and a half times her rate for six of her hours. She did the arithmetic on the back of a receipt and looked at the difference between what she had assumed and what the law said she was owed, and the difference was not enormous, but it was hers.

The next morning she asked the assistant manager, a tired man named only in her head as Terry-from-the-office, whether the extra hours would be paid differently. He said the system "usually catches it" and turned back to the invoices. She stood there for a moment, unsure whether she had been answered or brushed aside. On her break she told Flora, who was waiting by the customer service desk with a slushie. "Legally they have to pay you one and a half times your regular rate for hours over forty in a workweek," Flora said, reading off Anais's phone. "That's federal. So just check your paycheck."

"I don't want to be the person who makes a thing of it my third week," Anais said. "They might not have me back over break."

"They're short-handed. They need you more than you need them."

Anais wasn't sure that was true, and she said so. She thought about Chase, who would say that accepting the smaller check was exactly how a person's expectations ossified, how a whole workforce learned to expect nothing. She thought about her coworker at the register, who had once mentioned, dryly, that she'd stopped reading her pay stubs years ago; Anais had found that jaundiced at the time, and now found it maybe just tired. But she also knew that Terry had been kind to her, that the store had hired her when nowhere else called back, and that she did not want her first job to become, in her mind, a referendum on anything. She wanted it to be a job. She wanted the money. She wanted to be the kind of person who asked, once, plainly, and then knew how to read the answer.

Friday she was on register four when Chase came in to buy trail mix and argue, in his loose way, that she was already being shaped by the place. She rang him up while he talked, and she found she could listen without agreeing and disagree without fighting, which felt new. He called her an ideologue once, in their junior year, when she had refused to shop at a certain store, and she had hated the word, and now she thought the opposite danger existed too: deciding in advance that nothing was worth asking about, that all bosses and all systems were the same wall. The wall wasn't the same everywhere. Some walls were just Terry in an office, tired, with a system that usually caught things.

When her paycheck came, she sat in the break room and unfolded the stub. There were two rates on it. Six hours printed at a number larger than the rest, larger by exactly half, and she understood that the system had caught it after all, or that someone had caught it, or that the law had held without her having to raise her voice, and she could not tell which, and decided that she would keep her eyes open anyway. She folded the stub along its old crease and put it in her back pocket. On her way back to register four she passed the office, and Terry looked up from his invoices, and she tapped her pocket once and said, "Thank you."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: A food bank is usually a central warehouse that collects and distributes food to local agencies, while a food pantry is where people pick up food directly.
story:
Jade had signed up because the scholarship form required forty hours of community service, and because Ms. Tse, who ran the warehouse on Delancey Street, had seemed like the kind of adult who would sign the form without asking questions. That was the whole plan. She had imagined handing bags of groceries to grateful strangers, something photogenic, something she could describe in an essay paragraph and then never think about again. Instead, on her first Saturday, she was sorting dented cans into a green plastic bin while a radio somewhere played staticky oldies.

"So when do the people come?" she asked Sean, who had been volunteering since September and wore a hairnet like it was nothing. Around them the warehouse stretched long and cold, pallets of rice stacked to the ceiling, forklifts beeping in the far aisles. It looked like a place where things arrived and left in trucks, not a place where anyone would come for dinner.

Sean laughed, not unkindly. "Nobody comes here for groceries. A food bank is the central warehouse. It collects the food and distributes it out to the agencies. The pantries are where people actually pick it up." He tossed a crushed can of peaches into the trash. "There's like thirty of them around the city."

Jade turned this over while she worked. She had been picturing the wrong place entirely, a room with folding tables and a line, and she felt a small embarrassment that she chose not to allay by pretending she had known all along. Before she could say anything more, the loading door scraped open and a man walked in, older, in a coat too heavy for October, his voice already raised before the door had finished moving.

"I need food," he said. "They told me downtown, come here, somebody here would have a box."

"We don't do boxes," said the driver, an irascible man everyone called only by his last name, and he said it in a tone that suggested the conversation was over. The visitor's shoulders stiffened, and Jade watched him begin the slow turn of someone about to leave with nothing, and she thought, abruptly, of Marcus Reyes in seventh grade.

Marcus had stood beside her at the vending machines with sixty cents and an expression he was trying to make blank, and she had looked away, had studied the chip selection like it fascinated her, and had let him walk off. It was such a small thing. She had told herself for years it was such a small thing that it barely counted as a choice, but she was seventeen now and could admit she had made it in half a second, and that she still remembered his sneakers.

She set down the can in her hand. "Wait," she said, to the man, to the driver, to the room. "There are pantries. Where people pick up food directly. We're the bank part." Sean was already pulling up a map on his phone, and Ms. Tse came over from the office with a printed list she kept for exactly this, apparently, because the list was soft at the edges from handling. The closest pantry was at a church on Fairmount, open until two.

"Can he get there?" Jade asked. Ms. Tse said the bus route ran straight up Fairmount, and Jade walked the man to the loading door and gave him the list, and he looked at her for a moment longer than was comfortable, and said, "You could've let me walk out." Then he did walk out, in the right direction, the list folded in his fist.

Later, stacking boxes of pasta with Sean, she tried to decide whether she had done something good or only something adequate. In her government class they had spent a week arguing about whether theocracy or democracy better protected the vulnerable, and Calista had claimed that systems mattered more than individuals, that kindness was unreliable, a weather system rather than a climate. Jade had half agreed then. She half agreed now. If the pantry closed at two and the bus ran late, her list was worth nothing; if the city funded the bank properly, maybe the man would not have been sent to the wrong door at all. Both things could be true. She did not know how to hold them at once, so she kept stacking, and Ms. Tse signed her form at the end of the shift and said, "Same time next week?" Jade looked at the empty loading dock where the man had stood.

"Same time next week," she said.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: Deuteronomy 22:8 commands building a parapet around a flat roof so that no one falls, and Jewish tradition extends the rule to other hazards on one's property.
story:
Megan set her phone on the counter, propped against the flour canister, and read the verse aloud for the fourth time. "When you build a new house, you shall make a parapet for your roof, so that you do not bring bloodguilt on your house if anyone should fall from it." Her mother was at the stove, browning onions, and the kitchen smelled like Tuesday, which was soup night, which was also now debate-prep night, because the tournament was in three days and the resolution was whether an ancient religious rule could still apply to modern life.

"You're going to argue about a roof," her mother said, without turning around.

"A flat roof," Megan said. "It's Deuteronomy 22:8. People in that part of the world used their roofs like we use porches. So the rule says, put a parapet around it, a low wall, so nobody falls." She scrolled to the notes she'd been assembling. "And it's not just roofs. Jewish tradition extends it to other hazards on your property. A broken step, an unfenced pool, a dog that bites. The principle travels."

Her mother stirred the onions and said nothing, which Megan understood as permission to keep going. She had been going for two days. Aariz had texted her a photo of his own debate outline with the caption "going full atheist historicist, wish me luck," which meant he would stand up on Saturday and argue that the rule was a tribal artifact, that people who kept it were keeping a museum, and that Megan, arguing the affirmative, would be cast as the fundamentalist. That was the part that stung. She wasn't religious in any way she could defend at a dinner table.

Curtis came over at six with a printout, because Curtis still printed things, and spread the pages across the kitchen table where the soup bowls would go in twenty minutes. "Here's your problem," he said, tapping a highlighted line. "Your whole case is one verse."

"It's not one verse if the tradition extends it. That's the point. The verse is the seed and the tradition is the growth. A rule from three thousand years ago becomes the reason you fence your pool in 2024."

Aariz arrived late, still in his soccer jacket, and dropped into the fourth chair. "I heard my name from the driveway," he said. "Or I heard my role. The one who vilifies the ancient world."

"Nobody's vilifying anyone," Megan said. "That's what I want to avoid. The whole debate always becomes: ancient people irrational, modern people enlightened. But look at this." She turned her phone toward him and read the verse again, then the line beneath it about the extension to other hazards. "That's a landlord being held responsible for what happens on his property. That's not superstition. That's a safety code with a theory of culpability attached. If someone falls because you didn't build the railing, the blood is on your house. Three thousand years early."

Aariz pulled one of Curtis's pages toward him and read for a while, and the kitchen went quiet except for the ladle and the small subterranean hum of the refrigerator that Megan only ever noticed in silences. "Okay," Aariz said finally. "But here's my counter. If the rule is good because it matches what we'd do anyway, then the rule isn't doing any work. You'd fence the pool without Deuteronomy. So either it's redundant or it's wrong, and either way you don't need it."

"That's actually the strongest thing anyone's said to me all week," Megan admitted, and Curtis looked wounded, so she added, "Present company excepted," though the exception wasn't really true.

They ate soup with the printouts pushed to one end of the table, and Megan kept writing on a napkin between spoonfuls, trying to find the shape of a position she could actually hold. What she kept circling back to was this: the verse didn't claim to be efficient. It claimed that a hazard on your property was your responsibility before anything went wrong, that you owed the parapet to a guest who hadn't arrived yet. She couldn't prove the ancient rule caused that idea rather than just recording it. But she could argue that carrying an old text forward, testing it against a modern case, was itself a way of thinking worth keeping, and she could be honest that she didn't know where the text's authority ended.

"You're going to concede uncertainty in a debate round?" Curtis said. "On purpose?"

"I'm going to say what I actually think," Megan said, "and see if it survives."

On Saturday the rounds went long, and by the final one Megan was tired enough to speak plainly, which turned out to be her best strategy all day. She laid out the parapet verse, the extension, the pool, the step, the theory of responsibility, and she conceded the part she couldn't know, and the judge wrote something that made her lean forward in her chair to try to read it upside down.

Aariz took first speaker. Megan took second, which was the same as losing, except that afterward a girl from another school came up to her in the hallway holding her own phone and said, "That roof thing. We just moved into a place with a balcony and no railing, and my dad keeps saying it's the landlord's problem. Can you send me the citation?"

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Minnesota's Department of Transportation says the zipper merge, using both lanes up to the merge point and then taking turns, can cut a backup's length by as much as 40 percent.
story:
The cones were still in the trunk when Cohen's mother pulled into the bank lot, two spaces short of the drive-through, and told him to make the deposit before the branch closed at five. His road test was at eight the next morning, and he had exactly one evening left to learn what three weeks of practice had not taught him: how to park between two objects without stopping six feet away from the curb, and how to merge onto a highway that everyone in his family described differently.

Inside, the line was short. Ahead of him stood Harris, holding a folded check and a phone he kept tilting toward the window, where Cohen's mother had begun setting up the cones, seven feet apart, using the empty end of the lot as a practice bay. "Is she expropriating the parking spots for the good of your driving career?" Harris asked. "Because that's my spot she's colonizing."

"Tomorrow morning," Cohen said. "Eight a.m. The test. I still can't parallel park."

"You can't merge either," said Abbigail, appearing beside them with a deposit slip of her own. "I was in the car Tuesday. You get on the entrance ramp and you drive like the highway owes you an apology."

The teller, Mr. Farah-Ali, counted Cohen's bills without hurry, money he had saved all summer for insurance, and slid the receipt across. "Test tomorrow?" he asked, because in a town this size everyone knew everyone's failures in advance. "You will be fine. My nephew failed twice. Then he passed."

"Thank you," Cohen said, though it was the kind of bromide that made failure sound like a phase of the moon, something that would pass on its own.

Out in the lot, he took the wheel while his mother stood by the cones and Harris and Abbigial watched from the curb. He backed in too shallow, corrected too hard, and finished at an angle that would have failed him for certain. The second attempt was worse. On the third, his mother tapped the asphalt with her toe where the curb would be, and he found the angle suddenly, the car settling straight between the cones with a foot of clearance he hadn't believed was there. He sat in the parked car for a moment, letting it be true.

"Okay," Abbigail said through the open window. "Now the merging. That's the part that's going to ruin you."

"I move over early," Cohen said. "As soon as I see the sign. That's polite. That's what my dad says."
