"My cousin in Minneapolis says that's wrong," Harris said. "Minnesota's Department of Transportation says the zipper merge, using both lanes up to the merge point and then taking turns, can cut a backup's length by as much as 40 percent."

Cohen repeated it to himself, both lanes up to the merge point, then taking turns, forty percent, because it sounded like the opposite of everything he had been taught. Merging early felt axiomatic to him, the way queueing felt axiomatic: you got in line the moment the line existed, and anyone who drove past the line was a cheater. He had ridden with his uncle past a construction merge, watching cars crawl forward in the right lane while a pickup sailed by on the left and cut in at the cones, and he had felt the justice of his uncle's horn.

"Taking turns," he said. "Like a zipper."

"Like a zipper," Harris said.

They drove out to the county road, where a lane closure had narrowed traffic to one lane near the bridge, orange signs warning of construction a half mile ahead. Most cars drifted immediately into the right lane, and Cohen's instinct was to follow them, to be good, to merge early and wait his turn behind sixteen strangers. Instead, at Abbigail's nod from the passenger seat, he stayed left. He drove past the waiting cars with his jaw tight, feeling like a thief, and then, at the point where his lane actually ended, he signalled, slowed, and a little sedan let him in, one car, one gap, the driver waving him forward almost cheerfully. Behind him, another car did the same, and then another, an alternating rhythm that no one had directed.

"It's working," Abbigail said, looking back at the shortened line behind them. "It's actually shorter."

He could see both sides of it now, or thought he could: the early merge was a courtesy in light traffic, when there was no backup to shorten, and the late merge was a courtesy in heavy traffic, though it looked like greed. Where the line fell between light and heavy he could not yet say, and he suspected no one could say it exactly, not his father, not the cousin in Minneapolis, maybe not the Department of Transportation either. What he knew was that the cones in the bank lot had surrendered to him three times out of six, and the zipper had worked once, in one place, on one evening.

They got burgers afterward and sat on the hood, and Harris quizzed him on hand positions until the light went orange over the road. At eight the next morning the examiner would slide into the passenger seat with a clipboard, and Cohen would either find the angle or he wouldn't. His mother took the keys when it was time to go home, and he watched the bank lot shrink in the mirror, the cones still standing at the far end like a small argument he had finally begun to answer.

"One more time before we turn," he said. "Pull over. Let me drive the last mile."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: In the United States the Federal Reserve's main policy rate is the federal funds rate, the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves.
story:
Alexandre had signed up to explain monetary policy to Ms. Barrett's economics class on Thursday, and by Monday he still could not say why raising a number made prices stop rising. The presentation was worth a quarter of the grade. He had a slide that said "The Fed raises rates, inflation cools," and beneath it a bullet point that said "Somehow." He deleted the bullet point, then put it back.

"Go to the actual bank," Keely said at lunch. "Banks have pamphlets. Banks love pamphlets."

"There's a branch two blocks from school," Drake said. "I have to deposit a check anyway. My grandmother sends me eleven dollars every birthday and I never spend it because spending it would mean the birthday is over."

The deadline was three days away. After last period they walked to the branch on Miller Street, where a television mounted above the teller windows was playing a news channel with the sound off. The closed captions said the Federal Reserve had raised rates again, and a man on screen stood in front of a building pointing at a chart.

Alexandre got in line behind Drake. When a teller called them up, Drake slid his check across and asked her, as an afterthought, "Hey, which rate does the Fed actually set? The TV says rates, plural, like they set everything."

"The federal funds rate," the teller said. "That's the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves." She stamped the check. "My husband explains it at every dinner. I could recite it in my sleep."

Alexandre wrote the sentence on the back of his hand while Drake asked whether the eleven dollars was safe. It was. On the sidewalk outside, Alexandre read his hand. Banks lending to banks, overnight, reserves. Not mortgages, not credit cards, not Drake's eleven dollars. The Fed set one thing, and everything else was a chain reaction he had drawn as a straight arrow.

He worked on it that night at his kitchen table, where his father was sorting receipts for the tax man and pretending not to hover. Alexandre drew the chain on graph paper. The Fed raises the federal funds rate, the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves; borrowing between banks gets more expensive; banks pass the cost along; loans get pricier everywhere; people and companies borrow less; they spend less; demand for everything eases; prices stop climbing so fast. He looked at it and thought it was too tidy. Real people were not arrows. He wrote "BUT" in the margin and could not finish the sentence.

At school Wednesday he cornered Keely in the library. "Here's my problem," he said. "The chain makes sense. But somewhere in the middle of it, actual people get squeezed. Someone with a credit card, someone trying to buy a car. It's not that the mechanism is cruel, exactly. It's that the mechanism doesn't know anybody."

"That's the whole thing you should say," Keely said. She pulled a book off the returns cart without looking at its title. "Present both. Here's how it works, and here's who it lands on. That's not weakness in a presentation, that's the presentation."

Ms. Barrett had once told them that economics was the study of choices under scarcity, and Alexandre had assumed she meant scarcity of money, but sitting in the library he began to think she meant scarcity of perfect options. Slowing inflation helped people whose wages were being eaten by prices, including the indigent, who had no savings to buffer anything. Higher rates hurt people mid-loan. The same lever touched both groups, and the people pulling it could not separate them. He said some of this out loud. Keely said, "Write it down before you forget it, you always say things better once and then ruin them."

Thursday he stood at the front with the graph paper taped to the whiteboard. "The Fed doesn't set your mortgage rate," he began. "It sets the federal funds rate, the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves. That sounds like a detail for bankers. It's the whole machine." He walked the class down the chain, arrow by arrow, and then he stopped at the margin where he'd written BUT, and finally read what he'd added at two in the morning: "Every link in this chain is a person deciding whether to wait." Drake raised his hand and asked whether his eleven dollars counted as reserves. Alexandre said no, and the class laughed, and he let it run for a second because it felt earned.

Afterward Ms. Barrett said the diagram was clear and the honesty was better than clear. Then she asked what he still didn't know, and he said, "Whether the pain lands on the right people, or just on the first people in line." She didn't write that on the rubric. She looked at it a moment, then handed back his graph paper and said, "Keep that page." He folded it into his binder, between the notes for a class he was no longer taking and a flyer for a swim club he'd never joined, and carried it out into the hall.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: Heating and cooling bills change with the seasons, so averaging a full year of bills gives a truer monthly cost than a single month's bill.
story:
The lease papers came by email an hour before Jason's bus reached his grandfather's house, and by the time he walked in smelling of diesel and cold, he had until tomorrow evening to put down a deposit on one of them. His grandfather was at the kitchen table with tea and a pencil sharpened to a stub, and behind him, on the counter, sat a shoebox of old envelopes, which Jason would not think to ask about until much later that night.

"The gray building's cheaper," Jason said, spreading his phone between the sugar bowl and the dish of walnuts. "Eight-fifty a month, utilities included. The one on Delancey is nine-twenty plus utilities, but Charlie's cousin lives there and says it's worth it."

His grandfather turned the phone toward the window light. "Included how? All of them? Heat, water, everything?"

"Utilities included," Jason read. "That's all it says."

He had planned to spend the weekend helping clear the garden beds, and he did, for a while, dragging tomato stakes to the burn pile while his grandfather sorted seed packets into rows and murmured about which had come true from seed and which hadn't, which plants showed themselves and which stayed hidden. Jason half listened. His mind kept circling back to the two apartments, to the strange arithmetic of being eighteen and about to commodify the place where he would sleep, eat, fail, and recover, as if a life could be priced by the square foot. The gray building was near Yaseen, which mattered. Delancey was near campus, which also mattered. Everything mattered and nothing added up.

After supper his grandfather cleared the table, went to the counter, and set the shoebox down beside the phone. Inside were twelve envelopes, one for each month, a year's worth of heating and cooling bills for the house. "You said utilities included," he said. "So ask what that costs them. Or ask what it would cost you." He tapped the August envelope, then the one beneath it, and left the room to wash up.

Jason opened the August envelope first, because it was on top, and the number was so small he actually laughed. He texted Charlie: gray building is a steal. Then, because there was nothing else to do until the wrestling came on, he opened September, and October, and worked through the stack the way his grandfather sorted seeds, laying them in rows, and the numbers climbed steadily toward a February envelope that made him sit very still. One month was a mirage. He wrote all twelve figures in his grandfather's spidery pencil, added them, divided by twelve, and the true monthly cost rose out of the pile like something surfacing. Summer had lied to him; only a full year told the truth. When he ran the same averaging on the cooling-heavy months for Delancey, using what Charlie's cousin could remember of her bills, the gap between the two apartments shrank to almost nothing.

His grandfather came back drying his hands. "Well?"

"It's basically a tie," Jason said. "The gray one only looked cheaper because I was holding summer in my hand."

"Then choose with something besides price." The old man sat, took off his glasses, and cleaned them with the hem of his cardigan, the way he did when he wanted a decision to be somebody else's. "Though prices are the easy part to get wrong. When your grandmother and I took the flat on Marsh Street, we counted the rent and not the stairs, and for four years she carried a bicycle up two flights."

Jason laughed, then stopped, because he was doing the same thing in reverse, counting stairs and not rent, counting Yaseen's proximity and not the hour-long commute to campus, counting the brick veneer of Delancey and not the thin walls Charlie's cousin complained about. Even the seedlings in the garden had been his grandfather's lesson on this, though the old man had never said so: plants grown from the same parents still showed themselves differently, and you didn't know which until the season turned. Jason had thought that was just biology homework talk. Now it sounded like leases.

He called his mother, who said the deposit was his decision and his money, which was its own kind of weight. Then he texted Yaseen: not the gray one, I don't think, I'll explain tomorrow. He set his alarm for seven, because the office opened at nine and the deposit was due by five. Before bed he stood at the back door looking at the empty beds where the tomatoes had been, twelve months of bills stacked and squared on the table behind him, one seed packet left faceup on the counter, its photograph promising a fruit it might or might not ever produce.

"Whichever one I pick," he said to the kitchen, to the boxes, to his grandfather still sitting there, "I could be wrong by February."

"Probably," his grandfather said, and dealt him the last of the walnuts.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: In England, the Tenant Fees Act 2019 caps most tenancy deposits at five weeks' rent when the annual rent is under £50,000.
story:
Sofia laid the letting agent's email open on her phone at the kitchen table and read it for the third time, as though the number might soften. The flat above Mr. Lin's shop was small, the rent was within reach of what she and her mother could manage, and then the last line: deposit required, two months' rent upfront, plus first month, payable before the keys change hands. Her mother stood at the sink, not turning around, and Sofia understood that the silence was its own kind of arithmetic.

"Two months," Sofia said. "That's over two thousand pounds before we even move in."

Her mother wiped her hands on a towel. "That's how it is. When we bought nothing and rented everything, it was always how it was."

The counterpoint to that memory, though, arrived a second later, from the doorway. Mr. Lin had come up the stairs with a plate of dumplings because he had heard, through the floor, that they were looking at the flat. He had owned the building for thirty years, had paid off the mortgage a decade ago, and sometimes talked about it the way other people talked about a war they had survived. "Every month, money went to the bank instead of to me," he said, settling into the third chair. "For twenty years. But at the end, the house was mine. With renting, the money goes and never comes back as anything."

Sofia had heard a version of this before, in the summer, when Karl's parents had explained over burgers why they were moving out of the city. They had sold their flat, and with the proceeds as a down payment, they could afford a mortgage on a place near the coast, because the down payment was what made the bank willing to lend at all. Karl had drawn it on a napkin: a small pile, then a bigger pile that you paid back slowly, month after month, with interest riding on top like a passenger. Sofia had thought it sounded grandiose then, all that talk of equity, and she thought so still, sitting in a rented kitchen where the tap dripped into a bowl someone had placed there years ago and never replaced.

"Mr. Lin," she said, "two months as a deposit. Is that normal?"

He pulled the plate of dumplings toward himself, considering. "For my building, the agent handles it. I sign what they send."

Sofia turned back to the phone. Two months was roughly eight and a half weeks of rent. Something about that figure bothered her, a splinter under the skin of the number, and she could not have said why until she found it: a page she remembered Kayson mentioning months ago, when his brother had been flat hunting in London and had read out the rules like a man reciting scripture. She searched, scrolling past forums full of people asking the same question in different accents of panic, and there it was. The Tenant Fees Act 2019, which she said aloud, slowly, because saying it made it real, capped most tenancy deposits at five weeks' rent when the annual rent was under fifty thousand pounds.

She did the sums on the back of an envelope, the way her mother did the weekly budget, in small careful columns. Five weeks was not eight and a half weeks. The agent was asking for more than the law allowed, and the difference was nearly six hundred pounds, which was two months of her Saturday job at the garden centre.

She called the agent before she could lose her nerve. Kayson had once told her that the trick with authority was not to cajole, not to be charming, just to state the thing plainly and then stop talking, and she did that now: she named the Act, she named the cap, and she waited. The voice on the other end went quiet, then said it would need to check with the landlord, then said, with the deflation of a punctured tyre, that yes, the deposit would be revised to five weeks. Sofia wrote it down while her mother watched from the sink, and Mr. Lin nodded as though a fair price had finally been named in his shop.

The email came that evening, while the dumplings were being reheated. The deposit was corrected, exactly as promised, and Sofia felt the brief flare of having won something. Below it, in a paragraph she had to read twice, was the rest: another applicant had come forward that afternoon, a couple, no children, offering the full asking rent for a two-year term, and the landlord, who was Mr. Lin's cousin and not Mr. Lin, had accepted their holding deposit. Sofia put the phone face down on the table.

"They gave it to someone else," she said.

Mr. Lin looked at his plate. Her mother sat down across from Sofia and took one of her hands, the way she used to when Sofia was small and the news was a dead goldfish, then a cancelled holiday, now this.

"So we stay here," her mother said. "Another year."

Sofia turned the envelope over, where the corrected sums still showed, five weeks, the right number at last, and slid it beneath the fruit bowl for next time.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: A 2019 study led by Ziad Obermeyer found a widely used US health-care algorithm underestimated Black patients' needs because it used past medical spending as a stand-in for how sick patients were.
story:
The permission slip said MedSystems Computing, and Marcus had signed it mostly for the free bus ride out of fourth period, though he'd told Ms. Silva he was considering their internship. He was, in the way you consider things you assume will reject you. In the building's atrium, a wall-sized screen cycled through animated water, tuna streaking through blue light, and Nya stood in front of it with her phone out, filming. "Pelagic fish," she said. "Open ocean. I'm doing my bio presentation on tracking tags, and this is better footage than anything I can find." She wanted the footage the way Marcus wanted the internship: quietly, and without permission to want it.

In the demo room, an engineer named only on her badge as Priya showed them a model that flagged hospital patients for extra care. Faye, who had been quiet all morning, raised her hand. "How do you know what your data label really measures?" she asked. "Like, how do you know the number means the thing you think it means?" Priya paused, then said it was the best question anyone had asked on a tour all year. She told them about a 2019 study led by Ziad Obermeyer: a widely used US health-care algorithm had underestimated Black patients' needs because it used past medical spending as a stand-in for how sick patients were. "People spent less on them, so the algorithm decided they were less sick. The label wasn't health. It was money."

On the bus back, Marcus wrote that down in his notebook, twice, because his handwriting got worse when he was thinking. Ms. Silva had assigned the class a project: build a model on the county's public dataset that predicted which students were "at risk" of not graduating, and present it in two weeks. Marcus had planned to use attendance, referrals, and library checkouts, the columns with the cleanest numbers. Now he sat with the worksheet open on his knee and did not write anything.

In the computer science classroom the next morning, the machines booted in their staggered, elderly way, and Faye dropped into the seat beside him. She had her own agenda, which she stated plainly: Ms. Silva had agreed to write her letter of recommendation for the state scholarship, but only after seeing her project, and Faye intended to build something good enough that the letter practically wrote itself. "I'm labeling kids by lunch status," she said. "Free and reduced. It's the strongest predictor in the dataset." She said it the way you'd report a weather forecast.

Marcus ran the numbers anyway, because he wanted to see. The model worked, in the sense that its accuracy was high, and for a moment that felt like the whole argument. Then he pulled up the column descriptions and found that "at risk" had been assigned by guidance counselors based on whether a student had been recommended for intervention, and he remembered Priya saying the label wasn't health, it was money. He ascribed too much to the number, he thought, or the school had. He couldn't yet tell which of them was more at fault, or whether fault was even the right frame for a column header somebody had typed years ago.

"Check this," he said to Faye, angling his screen. "Our label isn't 'didn't graduate.' It's 'someone decided to worry about them.' Same problem as the health thing. Students who don't get noticed don't exist in the training data." Faye frowned at the screen, then at him, then pulled her chair over. Nya appeared behind them with her headphones around her neck, having given up on her tracking-tag footage for the period. "So who's missing?" she asked. "Not who's flagged. Who never got a file at all." They spent the rest of the period writing queries to find students with sparse records, the ones the system had barely touched.

When Ms. Silva stopped at their row, Marcus explained, haltingly, that he wanted to present the model alongside its own failure, that accuracy was doing exactly what the health-care algorithm had done, standing one thing in for another. He was honest about what he couldn't resolve: he didn't know how to fix it, only how to show it. Ms. Silva asked whether that was enough. "I don't know yet," Marcus said. Faye had gone still beside him, and he realized she was weighing her letter against his idea, the clean impressive model against the messy true one. She exhaled. "We do it together," she said. "The mess. I want my name on the mess."

The morning of the presentation, Marcus got to the classroom early and found the screen saver on the front monitor playing the ocean, Nya's footage, uploaded sometime in the night. Tuna moved through open water, untagged, going wherever they went. He set his slides to load and watched the fish until the first bell rang and Faye came through the door carrying the projector cable. "Ready?" she said. He pressed the spacebar, and the first slide came up white, with only a question on it: "What does our label actually measure?"

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: For ideal parallel plates, the field also equals the charge per unit area on a plate divided by the permittivity of free space, about 8.85 × 10^-12 farads per metre.
story:
The problem on Daniel's desk had been staring back at him for twenty minutes. Two parallel plates, a charge given in microcoulombs, an area in square metres, and a point P marked neatly between them. What it did not give was a voltage, and every formula he knew wanted one. He had circled the missing number twice, hard enough that the pencil tore a little crescent in the paper.

His phone buzzed beside his elbow. A message from Norman: "mr wilson is out sick. sub collected the hw but didn't check it. did you get 6b? the one with the plates?" Daniel typed back that he was on it, then deleted "on it" because it was a small lie, and sent "stuck on it" instead. Norman replied with a single word, "same," and then, a minute later, "nathanael says he finished early and it took him like ten minutes, which is a very nathanael thing to say."

Daniel got up and went to the kitchen, where his mother was chopping onions for something that would take hours. He stood at the counter and explained the problem to her, partly because talking it out helped and partly because she asked. He said that between two charged plates the field was usually the voltage divided by the distance, which he could recite in his sleep, and that the worksheet gave him no voltage at all. "So the whole question is a kind of oxymoron," he said. "A field problem with the field's ingredients missing." She said that sounded like his grandfather's crossword puzzles, and that missing ingredients were usually hiding somewhere else in the cupboard.

He carried an apple back to his room and sat down again at the desk, which was really the end of his bed with a board across it. He opened his textbook to the chapter on capacitors and read past the highlighted boxes, past the worked examples, into the dense paragraphs he usually skipped because they felt parochial, all about one narrow setup that would never come up again. Except it had come up again, tonight, on his desk.

There it was, one sentence, almost offhand. For ideal parallel plates, the field also equalled the charge per unit area on a plate divided by the permittivity of free space, which the book gave as about 8.85 × 10 to the minus 12 farads per metre. He read it three times. He had the total charge and the area, so he could divide one by the other, and then divide that by the 8.85 number, and out would come the field with no voltage needed at all. The problem wasn't broken. It was just asking him to come in through the back door.

He checked his units on a scrap of paper, dividing and cancelling until he was left with newtons per coulomb, which was what a field was supposed to be, and then he did the arithmetic twice because the exponent was small enough to hide a mistake. When he had a number he believed, he picked up his phone and typed a long message to Norman, explaining the whole route: the charge per unit area, the permittivity, the value 8.85 × 10^-12 farads per metre, the answer at point P. He ended it with "check my exponent, I don't trust myself past 10^-4." He hit send before he could soften it.

Norman's reply came while Daniel was copying the solution into neat. "wait. so you don't need the voltage at all?" Then: "that's messed up. they never said we could do that." Daniel wrote back that the book said it, in the part nobody reads, and that maybe the point was to make them read it. Norman sent a thumbs up and then, unexpectedly, a second message: "my dad wants me to drop physics and take business instead next year. he thinks it's parochial, like it only leads to one job. showing him this. the back door thing." Daniel read that twice, hearing Norman's voice in it, the argument he was clearly having at his own kitchen table a mile away.

Daniel sat with the phone in his hand, thinking that he hadn't internalized the formula yet, not really; he had used it once and it had worked, and tomorrow Mr. Wilson would return and maybe confirm it or maybe point out some catch about real plates versus ideal ones that the book had buried even deeper. He wrote "tell your dad physics people also invent the stuff business people sell" and then deleted it, because it sounded like a poster, and sent "it worked tho" instead, which was smaller and truer.

He copied the final answer into the box on the worksheet, put a star beside it, and texted Nathanael the number, adding, "verify?"

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: English newspaper headlines often drop small words like 'the' and use the present tense for past events, a compressed style sometimes called 'headlinese'.
story:
Leo had the newspaper folded to a single column on the counter of the restaurant, holding it flat with one hand while the other warmed around a coffee cup that was not his. He was allowed to sit at the far booth until the dinner rush, and after that he bussed tables, refilled water, and kept the folded page in his apron pocket, where it went soft at the creases.

The article was short, maybe two hundred words, about a mayor who had opened a footbridge over the canal the day before. His tutor had assigned it: read it, then summarize it aloud, in his own words, in under a minute. The summary he had drafted on a napkin ran to three napkins. Lexi had read one and told him it was prolix, which he had looked up that night, and which he suspected was the polite version of something worse.

The headline was the part that defeated him. "Mayor Opens Bridge Over Canal." He had read it forty times during the lunch shift, waiting for the grammar to arrive. In his own language you could not say this. The mayor opens the bridge, perhaps, if he did it every morning, the way someone opens a shop. But the article said clearly that he had done it yesterday, with scissors, in the rain, once. And there was no the anywhere, no a, nothing holding the words to each other. It looked like the English of someone who had learned English from a ransom note.

Phoebe slid into the booth across from him, stealing a sugar packet without asking. She was studying linguistics in the fall and liked to practice on him the way other people practiced piano on whatever room they happened to be in. He pushed the paper toward her and said, "This headline. It has no grammar. It is broken English and it is in a real newspaper."

She read it twice and laughed, not unkindly. "It's called headlinese," she said. "They drop the little words like the, and they use the present tense for things that already happened."

"So it means the opposite of what it says."

"It means exactly what it says. You just have to know the rules for how it says it." She tapped the napkin summaries, which had begun to curl from the steam of the kitchen. "Your problem is the reverse. You write everything. The mayor, who is a man, and who on the previous day, in the rain, which was falling."

He argued for a while that this was safer, that in his language precision was politeness, that dropping words felt like dropping the handrail on a staircase. She said that was pragmatics, context doing half the work, and he did not fully follow her, but he wrote both words down. Behind the counter the pickles Mr. Quinn made in the back room were fermenting in their jar, and the whole restaurant smelled faintly of them, and Leo thought his understanding was something like that, sitting in a brine, quietly becoming what it was going to become.

He practiced on the dinner customers, in his head, while he carried plates. Woman Returns Lost Wallet. Kitchen Runs Out of Salmon. He liked the compression, the way it made the whole shift into a series of small headlines, each one finished before his arms got tired. When the rush thinned, Mr. Quinn came in for his usual and sat at the counter, and Leo, still holding the towel, summarized the article aloud to him: mayor, footbridge over the canal, opened yesterday, ribbon cut in the rain, small crowd, complaints about the cost. Under a minute. Full sentences, the little words included. Mr. Quinn listened all the way through without checking his phone, which he had never done before, and said it was the best thing he'd heard all week, and told Leo he ought to write for the paper instead of waiting tables.

After Mr. Quinn had gone, Leo read his napkin summaries one last time and tore them up, feeling both lighter and slightly poorer, the way he did whenever he threw away something he had made. Phoebe leaned over the counter to take the last sugar packet. "Table four," she said. "You told them soup is off."

"Is off. Yes. It is off."

"You said, 'Kitchen runs out of soup.' They thought it was, like, a daily announcement. They asked if it comes back tomorrow."

Leo looked down at his hands, still holding the towel, then at the torn napkins in the trash, every careful word of them gone.

"Tell them," Phoebe said, "the soup is gone, the kitchen is sorry, and the the is on the house."

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: Many parliamentary systems separate the head of state, such as a monarch or ceremonial president, from the head of government, while in the United States the president is both.
story:
Nathan arrived at the community centre with the debate cards rubber-banded against his thigh, and the clock above the gym door already read 6:52. The student government's mock constitutional convention began at seven, and he had promised Ms. Liu he would run the comparison station: two folding tables, a cardboard ballot box, and a hand-drawn diagram he had stayed up finishing, the ink still tacky at the corners. Outside, rain ticked against the tall windows, and the hallway smelled of floor wax and someone's microwave noodles.

Siena waved him over from the table where she was taping signs. "You're cutting it close," she said. "Cyris already tried to rearrange your stations. He thinks the parliamentary one should come first."

"Cyrus," Nathan corrected, out of habit. He set down his cards and looked at the gym, which had been transformed overnight from a badminton court into something resembling a very small country. Two flags borrowed from the drama department hung at the far end, neither of them real, which struck Nathan as fitting. He unrolled his diagram and weighted the corners with badminton tubs.

Cyrus appeared with a stack of pamphlets and an argument he had clearly rehearsed. "Your setup makes it look like they're the same thing with different hats," he said. "A prime minister and a president. Kids are going to walk away thinking it's just vocabulary."

"It kind of is vocabulary," Nathan said, and heard how weak it sounded even before Cyrus's eyebrows went up.

The first visitors came through at 7:10, mostly freshmen dragged in for extra credit, moving in packs. Nathan walked them through the presidential side first because that was what they knew: the whole country votes, the winner gets the office, and removal means impeachment, a long and public business. Then he moved them to the other table. A girl with a lanyard around her wrist stopped him there, frowning at his diagram, where he had drawn a crown hovering above a smaller box.

"Wait," she said. "My cousin lives in England. They have a king. So who's in charge?"

"Both, sort of," Nathan said. "Many parliamentary systems separate the head of state, like a monarch or a ceremonial president, from the head of government. In the United States, the president is both." He pointed at the crown and then at the smaller box, which he had labelled with a prime minister's functions, and the girl nodded slowly, the way people nod when something has clicked into place without quite being able to say why.

Cyrus, who had drifted over with his pamphlets, said, "See, that's the part you buried at the bottom of your diagram. That should be the first thing they hear." He tapped the crown. "It's modularity. You've got the country split into two boxes, one for symbolism and one for actually governing. The American system just refuses the split."

Nathan had not thought of it that way, and the realization irritated him, because Cyrus had found the shape of the idea in about nine seconds while Nathan had spent two evenings arranging facts without seeing the architecture underneath. He tried to externalize what he was feeling, some of it, anyway. "I put it at the bottom because it seemed like a technicality," he admitted. "I thought the interesting part was how they remove each other. Votes of no confidence versus impeachment."

"That's interesting too," Siena said, sliding past with a roll of tape. "But you can't take apart the engine until you show them there are two engines."

The convention's clock ran down toward the open forum at 8:30, when the students would vote on which system their imaginary country should adopt, and Ms. Liu had told Nathan he would give the closing comparison before the vote. Eight minutes. He sat on the stage steps with his cards and found he could not make them fit the order he had rehearsed. His arrangement suddenly felt subterranean, like the real logic had been buried under his own sequencing, and Cyrus's version kept surfacing in his mind no matter how he pushed it down.

He thought about his father, who used to say that if you wanted to know whether a machine was well designed, you watched what happened when it broke. Nathan had loved that as a kid, mostly for the permission to break things. Now it seemed like half a principle at best, because a machine that breaks rarely tells you why it was built that way, only what its designer feared.

Ms. Liu appeared at the edge of the stage and held up five fingers. Nathan stood, tucked his old cards into his back pocket, and walked to the podium with only the diagram, which he propped on the music stand. He looked out at the folding chairs, at Siena giving him a thumbs up and Cyrus leaning against the wall with his arms crossed, and he began where the crown was.

"This is the head of state," he said, tapping it. "And this is the head of government. Some countries keep them in two separate boxes. Ours doesn't."

"Which one's better?" someone called from the third row.

Nathan looked at the clock, then back at the crowd. "Vote and find out."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The yellow first-down line shown on televised American football is computer-drawn; it was first broadcast on ESPN on September 27, 1998, by a company called Sportvision.
story:
The screen door of Mr. Martínez's house slapped shut behind Jack, and the noise of the party folded over him like a warm coat. The big game was already on, twenty-two bodies colliding in high definition, and everyone had gathered in the den because Mr. Martínez had the largest television on the street and the generosity to go with it. Jack's father claimed the good chair. Myah and Carina took the floor with paper plates of chips, and Jack's little cousin, nine years old and vibrating with soda, wedged himself against Jack's knee.

"Watch this," the cousin said, pointing at the screen with a nacho. "See the yellow line? That's how far they have to go."

"I know how a first down works," Jack said.

"No, I mean it's painted on the field. Yellow paint. The players can see it."

Jack looked at the line, that impossible stripe of gold lying across the grass, and felt something itch at the back of his mind. He had watched hundreds of games and never once asked himself how the line stayed so crisp while men stamped across it, how it vanished the instant the play ended. Paint did not behave that way. Paint did not know where the chains were.

"It's not paint," Carina said from the floor, without looking up.

"How do you know?"

"Because the players would slide on it, genius."

"That's not proof," Myah said, and Jack appreciated her for that, the refusal to accept a good answer for the wrong reason. The cousin, however, was unmoved. He announced that he would bet his dessert, his Halloween candy, and one dollar that the line was real, physical, down there among the cleats. Fourth quarter began in forty minutes. Jack, who had a dollar and an appetite for being right, accepted the deadline.

While the defense huddled, Jack borrowed Mr. Martínez's phone. He found what he was looking for in two searches, and it was stranger than he expected. The yellow line was drawn by a computer, laid onto the broadcast the way weather maps got their rain. It had first appeared on ESPN on September 27, 1998, and the company that did it was called Sportvision. He read the sentence twice. Something that felt as ancient and permanent as the chalk of a baseball diamond, as much a part of the ground as the yard lines themselves, was younger than he was. His whole life, that line had been a fiction the television told him, and he had never once thought to doubt it.

He turned to his cousin. "Okay. It's not on the field. It's not painted anywhere. It's drawn on the screen, by a computer, before the picture gets to the TV."

"No way."

"The first time anyone ever saw it was on ESPN, September 27, 1998. A company called Sportvision made it."

The cousin stared at the screen with the betrayed expression of someone learning that a magician's coin came from a sleeve. "But it looks so," he began, and then went lugubrious, shoulders sagging, as if the whole game had been drained of something. Jack knew the feeling. He had felt it himself, flipping between the broadcast and the memory of every game he had watched as a kid, the two versions refusing to quite codify into one. Which was the real field: the green rectangle with bodies on it, or the one with the golden promise running through it?

Yet sitting there, listening to Myah argue with Carina about whether knowing a trick ruined it or made it better, Jack found he could not pick a side cleanly. The line was a lie and it was also the truest thing on the screen, because it told you exactly what mattered, what every person in that stadium and every viewer in every den actually cared about. Football had existed for most of a century without it, a whole antiquity of squinting at referees and chain crews, and now the yellow line felt like it had always been there. Both things were true at once, and he did not know how to hold them except to keep watching with both facts in his hands.

Mr. Martínez leaned over during the two-minute warning. "You settle that bet yet?"

"He owes me a dollar," Jack said.

"Two dollars," said the cousin. "It's two quarters left."

The running back took the handoff, plunged through the pile, stretched the ball toward an end zone neither of them could measure, and the crowd in the den rose all at once, shouting at a line only they could see.
